activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
Megan arrived at the bowling alley eleven minutes early, which she decided to treat as a coincidence rather than a symptom. She had spent the drive rehearsing openings, discarding each one, and by the time she pulled into the lot only two candidates survived: a joke about the shoes, or nothing. The shoes were doing their own work anyway, orange and brown, laced by some previous customer into a knot that suggested despair.

Bilal was already inside, standing at the counter with his own rented pair dangling from two fingers. He had texted her once that afternoon, a single message that said "see you at 7," which she had read nine times. Now he raised the shoes in a small salute, and she went to the counter, where the cashier handed over a pair in her size without comment, as though the whole transaction were too banal for ceremony.

They bowled badly, which helped. He rolled two gutters in a row and narrated both with the gravity of a documentary voiceover, and she laughed in a way that surprised her, unguarded, the sound arriving before she could approve it. By the third frame the conversation had found its footing: classes, the college he was starting in the fall, the fact that her mother had once been briefly famous in a local bowling league. But by the sixth frame it began to falter, and by the eighth it had died entirely, and they stood at the ball return watching a stranger's purple ball glide past on its way to lane fourteen.

"This is the part where we talk about weather," Bilal said. "Or we don't."

"Or we don't," Megan said. Then, because the silence was going to resuscitate itself as small talk if she didn't act, she took out her phone. "Okay. My friend Ashleigh told me about this thing. In 1997 there was a psychologist, Arthur Aron, and he had pairs of strangers take turns asking each other thirty-six questions that got gradually more personal. The pairs who did that ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk."

"So this is a study."

"This is a study that we are going to steal."

He considered the lane, the pins, the situation. "Do we have to be strangers?"

"Close enough. We've known each other for a conversation and a half." She pulled up the questions, which Ashleigh had sent her a link to in June with the note "for emergencies." "Question one. Given the choice of anyone in the world, whom would you want as a dinner guest?"

"Easy. My grandfather. He died before I could ask him anything important." He said it lightly, the way people set down heavy things, and she understood that the lightness was the point. "Your turn."

"David Attenborough," she said. "Because he'd make my mediocre pasta sound like a discovery."

They traded questions between frames, and the game deteriorated accordingly, since it is difficult to bowl well while disclosing what you would most regret not having done by forty. He said he regretted quitting piano out of spite at his own hands rather than any lack of love for it. She said, at question nineteen, that she was afraid she'd chosen her college for reasons she could defend but not feel, and that she had been trying for months to reconcile the two, to hold the sensible version of herself and the wanting one in the same hand without dropping either. He didn't offer a solution. He said, "Both of those sound like you," and there was a consonance between that and something she had privately suspected, a note sounding the same in two different instruments.

By question twenty-eight, the study's own number forgotten in favor of whatever they were actually doing, they had stopped bowling altogether. They sat on the carpeted bench behind the lane, shoes still on, the scoreboard cycling through its animated celebration of a strike neither of them remembered rolling.

"Here's what I can't tell," Megan said. "Whether the questions are doing it, or whether they're just a permission slip, and I would have felt this close anyway if either of us had been brave enough on our own." She had been turning this over since question twelve. The study, she thought, argued one way; her own experience, sitting here with her heart going fast in a fluorescent-lit bowling alley, argued something less tidy, some version where the questions worked and also weren't the whole of it, and she could not make the two ideas lie flat against each other.

"That's very perspicacious of you," Bilal said. "For the record."

"For the record, I think you just wanted to use that word."

"I've been saving it since tenth grade. I was hoping for a perspicacious moment and you finally provided one." He was smiling, but he let a beat pass, and then he said, "I don't know either. Maybe that's question thirty-six."

They still had eight to go, by Ashleigh's count, by Aron's count, by whatever count mattered. Megan looked at the scoreboard, at the little animated pin waving its arms in permanent congratulation, and then at him.

"Question twenty-nine," she said. "Your turn to ask."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Negative space is the empty area around and between the subjects of an image, and artists often draw that space to get a shape's outline right.
story:
Luca had the table by the window, the good one with the afternoon light, and he had held it for two hours with nothing to show except eleven bad chairs. The assignment was due Monday: draw an ordinary object, make it look solid, make it look like something you could sit on without falling through. His chairs kept falling through. The legs wandered, the seat tilted, the back curved like something melting. He sharpened his pencil until it was mostly shavings and started a twelfth.

Derek dropped into the chair across from him and spun the sketchbook around. "That's a chair having a crisis," he said.

"It's a chair that hates me." Luca pulled the book back. Across the room, Liliane was photocopying something, the machine flashing its green light at regular intervals, and Ms. Le was wheeling a cart of returns toward the stacks with the quiet authority of someone who had shushed them twice already.

"Then draw something else. Draw a brick."

"The assignment says an object we use every day. I use the chair every day. It should be easy." He said it and heard how it sounded, like the sentence itself was the lie, a small domestic mendacity he told himself in the library and would tell Ms. Aldana on Monday if he turned in a melting chair. Derek had already gone back to his phone, thumbs moving, his truculent hunch suggesting he would defend the window seat against all comers.

Liliane came over with her warm photocopies and looked at the sketchbook for a long moment, head tilted. She didn't laugh, which Luca counted as a kindness. "You keep staring at the chair," she said. "Like it's going to confess."

"It's not."

"Try staring at what isn't the chair." She tapped the white between two legs, the wedge of window showing through the back slats. "I read about a guy who taught drawing. He'd have students draw the gaps first."

"The gaps."

"Negative space," she said, as if naming a band. "The empty parts. Around and between things." She took a fresh sheet from his bag before he could argue and drew the shape of the window between the chair's legs, then the not-chair triangle under the seat, then the little rectangles of light through the slats. Slowly, on her page, an outline appeared that was unmistakably a chair, drawn by way of everything the chair was not.

Luca felt something in his chest palpitate, absurdly, like the photocopy machine's green pulse. He took the pencil. He drew the floor shapes around the feet, the air around the crest of the back, and where the shapes met, the chair's outline arrived on its own, truer than anything he had chased for two hours. He filled in the gaps like a jigsaw of absence, and when he finally outlined the chair inside them, it stood. It stood the way an actual chair stands, patient, holding its weight. He kept going, hunched, forgetting Derek, forgetting the time, until Ms. Le passed and set the returns cart down.

"We close in twenty minutes," she said, and then she looked. She looked long enough that Luca sat back. "The gap under the seat," she said. "You got the slant right. People always get that slant wrong."

The twist came Monday, or rather Sunday night, when he spread both drawings on his bedroom floor: his eleven failures, then the finished page, and saw that the finished page barely showed a chair at all. He had shaded the empty shapes dark and left the chair itself white, so the object was a pale ghost held together by all the space around it, and he could not decide whether he had drawn a chair or drawn its absence, whether the assignment was completed or sidestepped, whether the difference even mattered. He decided, lying there, that he would hand it in and say only what was true: that he could not draw the chair, so he had drawn everything else. He was still not sure it was a chair. He was sure it was the best thing he had ever made, and that these two certainties could sit in him at once, like the light and the dark on the page.

On Monday he carried it to the front of the room flat against his chest, and when Ms. Aldana asked what it was, he turned it around and said, "Look at what's around it first."

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Marxist historian Albert Soboul argued the Revolution was the moment the bourgeoisie overthrew feudal society and became the dominant class.
story:
The library smelled of warm dust and the lemon spray the custodian used on the tables on Fridays, and Angelina had spread her books across two of them anyway. She was three days into the historiographical essay and had learned exactly one thing: that historians had been arguing about the French Revolution for two hundred years and had not finished. The assignment asked her to trace how views of it had changed since 1800, and every source she opened seemed to disagree with the last. Mae sat across from her with a highlighter going dry in her hand, watching Angelina rearrange the same four note cards.

"You're shuffling them like they're going to shuffle themselves into an essay," Mae said.

"I'm thinking." Angelina laid the cards flat. One said 1789, one said feudalism, one said bourgeoisie, and one said only Soboul?, with the question mark pressed so hard into the card it had gone through. She had copied the sentence from a museum label on the class trip in October, a small brass plate beneath a portrait of a stern man in a cravat. 1789: a bourgeois revolution, the label had said, and she had stood there wondering whose idea that was, and then copied it down because the coach had been counting heads. It had sat in her binder for months before it became the center of this.

Eliza arrived carrying a stack of photocopies and set them down with the confidence of someone who had already written her conclusion. "I'm doing the whole thing on how the narrative changed after the fall of the Berlin Wall," she said. "Before that, everyone read the Revolution as a class story. After, they didn't." She said it the way she said most things, as though the matter were settled and Angelina was welcome to catch up.

Angelina turned over the card with the question mark. In the reading Ms. Georgiou had pulled for her that morning, an article published in the 1980s, she had found the name attached to her museum label. Marxist historian Albert Soboul argued the Revolution was the moment the bourgeoisie overthrew feudal society and became the dominant class. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, and felt the strange satisfaction of a name finally arriving for something she had been carrying around unlabeled. She had stood in front of a portrait in October holding somebody's argument without knowing it was an argument at all. It had looked like the building's opinion.

"Soboul," she said aloud.

"Who?" Mae leaned over the table.

"The museum. The label that called it a bourgeois revolution. That was his view, or grew out of it. Albert Soboul. He was a Marxist. He said 1789 was the moment the bourgeoisie overthrew feudal society and became the dominant class." She heard herself saying it and realized the sentence had transfigured her little card: the question mark was gone, and in its place was a person, a position, a whole way of seeing.

Eliza, who disliked being interrupted mid-thesis, looked petulant for a moment, then pulled one of her photocopies from the stack. "He's in here," she said, softer. "The revisionists went after him. Said there wasn't really a unified bourgeoisie, that the lines between classes were blurlier than he claimed." She slid the page across. "Here. And then the post-revisionists went after them." She smiled a little, sheepish. "It's arguments all the way down."

Angelina read the page, and then the one after it, and found that the essay she had been unable to start was assembling itself without her permission. There was Soboul's version, monumental and orderly, classes moving like weather fronts. There was the counter-version, messier, full of people who did not fit their categories. And there was her own problem, the one she would have to be honest about in the last paragraph: she could not tell, from where she sat in a library in her last year of school, which account was true, or whether true was even the right demand to make of either. She could only describe the argument and place herself carefully inside its edges. She picked up her pen and wrote across the top of a fresh card, in careful letters, a neophyte's first real sentence of the essay: Views of the Revolution did not simply accumulate; they turned on each other.

Ms. Georgiou passed behind them on her rounds, straightening a chair, saying nothing. Outside the tall windows the October light was going amber on the parking lot. Angelina lined up her cards, turned to a clean page, and began to write, "In 1800, the Revolution was still an open wound; by the time Albert Soboul wrote, it had become a structure."

"Is that your intro?" Mae asked.

Angelina looked at the sentence, and at the half-dry highlighter Mae held out to her anyway, as if to say it was still available. "It's a start," she said, and took it.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In her 2017 book 'Radical Candor', Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly.
story:
Charles had read the sentence three times before he believed it, and even then he kept the book open on his knee as if it might change its mind.

Kim Scott, 2017, Radical Candor. The argument was almost insultingly simple: good feedback meant caring personally about someone and challenging them directly, both at once. He had photographed the page with his phone in the library, partly so he could send it to Jonas and partly, he suspected, so he would have proof that such a thing had ever been stated out loud.

At dinner his mother set down a dish of rice and asked what he was smiling at, and he said nothing, and his father asked about the weekend tournament, and the smile went away.

The tournament had ended on Saturday with Jonas dropping the ball twice in the last quarter and Charles saying nothing at all. Not a word. He had patted Jonas's shoulder afterward, told him they'd get them next time, and then watched him repeat the same mistake at Sunday's practice because nobody had told him his feet were wrong. Mr. Pérez, who coached them on weekends and never said much, had pulled Charles aside in the parking lot and asked, quietly, whether he thought silence was a kindness. Charles had said he didn't want to embarrass his friend. Mr. Pérez had looked at him for a long moment and said nothing back, which was somehow worse.

The dinner was one of those interminable affairs where his grandmother's stories looped and his uncle argued with the radio, and Charles pushed rice around his plate and thought about Jonas's feet. The problem wasn't effort. Jonas worked harder than anyone on the team; he stayed late, he ran extra laps, he asked the younger players to hit balls at him until his forearms were red. The problem was that when the throw came in fast from the left, Jonas stepped back instead of forward, and every time he did it, the receiver paid for it.

Charles's phone buzzed under the table. Jonas: can u practice tomorrow before school? Charles looked at the message for a long time. It would be easy to reply yes and show up at seven and hit grounders at him until the streetlights went out, and it would be easier still to keep his mouth shut about why, to let the extra reps speak for themselves, as if repetition alone could unlearn a habit nobody had named.

There was a contrivance available to him, and he could see its shape clearly: praise the effort, bury the correction inside some general encouragement, hope Jonas figured it out through inference. That was what most people did. That was what Charles had done for two seasons. And it had cost them, Saturday most recently but also in the spring, when a district semifinal turned on the same small step backward and Jonas had stood in the outfield afterward looking like a boy waiting for someone to tell him what he'd done so he could fix it, and nobody had.

"Pass the beans, please," his grandmother said, and he passed the beans.

He excused himself before dessert and called from the front hallway, keeping his voice low. Jonas answered on the second ring. There was a girl at his house, Charles could hear her laughing in the background, Chloe probably, who had been at the game and had filmed the second drop on her phone.

"Tomorrow works," Charles said. "But before we go, I want to tell you something, and I need you to hear the whole thing before you get mad."

"I'm not going to get mad."

"In the fourth quarter Saturday, both drops, the throws from the left side, you stepped back. Every time. Watch the film Chloe took and count your steps. You step back, and the ball gets there before you're set."

Silence on the line, long enough that Charles could hear the girl's laughter again, further away now, as if Jonas had walked into another room. "Nobody said anything," Jonas said finally, and it wasn't an accusation exactly, but it landed like one, and Charles let it land because it was true.

"I know. That's on me. I've been watching you do it for two seasons and saying nothing because I didn't want it to be weird." He paused. "But I've been reading this thing, this book. Radical Candor, it's called. The idea is you care personally and you challenge directly, both at once, not one instead of the other. I'm bad at the second part. I'm working on it."

Jonas was quiet again. Through the phone came the sound of a door closing. "Chloe kept saying she thought something was off with my footwork," he said. "She wouldn't say what."

"She didn't want it to be weird either. Nobody does. That's the whole problem."

"So tomorrow," Jonas said, and his voice had shifted into something Charles recognized, the flat, focused tone he used in the last quarter, "you hit everything from the left. Fast ones. And you count my steps out loud."

"Every one."

"Fine." A breath. "You could've told me in the spring."

"I know," Charles said. He stood in the hallway with the phone warm against his ear, the dinner noise still going behind him, and did not offer the excuse that came to him, because it was the same excuse he'd been making for two seasons and it had never once enfranchised Jonas to fix anything. "Six-thirty at the field. Bring the film."

He hung up, and through the front window he could see the streetlight coming on over the empty diamond at the end of the block, small and steady in the dusk.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Each transfer RNA carries one amino acid and has a three-base anticodon that pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA.
story:
The retake was Thursday morning, seven fifteen, and Sadie had already failed the transcription and translation unit once. She stood in the community garden behind the science wing with a card in each hand, waiting for Mr. Ross to finish dividing the class into molecules.

"You'll be messenger RNA," he said to April, holding out a long strip of paper with three-letter groups written along it. "Cory, you're a ribosome. Walk beside her and read her out loud." Then he turned to Sadie. "You're a transfer RNA. Pick a card."

Each card had an anticodon on one side and an amino acid name on the other, and there was a box of them on the folding table, fanned out like a deck someone had abandoned mid-game. Sadie picked one at random. Three letters, then the word leucine underneath.

"Why am I doing this in a garden?" she asked.

"Because the room was booked," Mr. Ross said, and walked off toward the eighth graders, who were fighting over watering cans.

The idea, as far as Sadie could reconstruct it from the worksheet, was that April would walk slowly along the brick path reading her codons, and Cory would repeat each one, and whoever held the matching card was supposed to step in, hand over the amino acid, and step back out. She hadn't read the whole worksheet. She'd read the first question, decided it was hopeless, and folded it into her pocket, where it had gone turgid with morning dew into a stiff little brick.

April started walking. "AUG," she said flatly, clearly wishing she were anywhere else.

"Methionine," Cory read off his cheat sheet. "Who has the anticodon for AUG?"

Nobody moved. April turned around. "This is stupid."

"It's a retake," Sadie said. "Everything about it is stupid. Walk."

April walked. "CUU."

Sadie looked down at her card. Three letters. She counted the match, felt something click, and stepped forward. "Me. This one. Leucine." She held the card out to Cory, who wrote the word on the growing chain of paper taped to his sleeve.

April watched her. "You knew that?"

"I know this one."

"You failed the test."

"I know this one," Sadie said again, and it came out harder than she meant.

They kept going. April read, Sadie matched, Cory collected. Somewhere around the sixth amino acid, Sadie noticed she wasn't counting letters anymore; she was hearing the codon the way she heard a friend's voice from down a hall, whole and immediate. When April said UGU, Sadie's hand was already in the box before she consciously knew why, pulling out cysteine.

"Since when are you good at this?" April said.

Sadie didn't answer, because the honest answer had two halves and she didn't want to equivocate with either of them. The first half was that she'd spent Tuesday night with the textbook open on her floor, not reading exactly, but staring at the diagram until it stopped being a diagram and started being a hallway she could walk down. The second half was that she still couldn't have written the essay question. Mr. Ross wanted them to explain why the cell does this, in order, with the vocabulary, and every time Sadie tried to outline the answer she ended up writing sentences like the cell wants to make protein, which the rubric penalized because it smuggled in teleology, purpose where there was only process. She'd looked the word up after seeing it scrawled in red across her first attempt. The cell doesn't want anything. It just does this, the way water runs downhill.

"UAA," April said.

Cory checked his sheet. "Stop codon. We're done." He held up the paper chain. "Whatever this is."

"It's a protein," Sadie said. "Probably not a real one."

"It's real," Mr. Ross said from across the garden, and Sadie couldn't tell whether he was correcting her or just talking.

The bell was going to ring in six minutes, and the retake was Thursday, and the gap between walking down the hallway in her head and writing the paragraph Mr. Ross wanted was the whole distance between a pass and another failure. She took the worksheet out of her pocket and unfolded it against the fence. Explain, in your own words, how the sequence of bases in DNA becomes a sequence of amino acids.

April came over, still wearing her paper strip. "So what do you write?"

"I don't know yet," Sadie said. She looked at the crumpled page, then at her card, still in her hand, the one that had carried a single amino acid and matched a single codon. "Maybe I write about this. You reading, me holding the card."

"That's not science," April said.

"It happened in a garden," Cory said, still examining his chain.

Sadie folded the worksheet once, carefully this time, along the original crease. "Give me your strip," she said. "I want to check something."

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: By specializing and trading, two countries can each end up consuming combinations of goods that lie beyond what they could produce on their own.
story:
Jacob had spread his homework across the frozen foods case, using it as a desk, because the fluorescent light above aisle six was better than the one in his bedroom. On the graph paper in front of him, two curved lines crossed like parentheses, and a point he had marked in red sat stubbornly outside one of them. He had checked the arithmetic three times. The point stayed where it was, beyond the curve, and according to everything Ms. Dhillon had said in class, that should have been impossible.

"You're blocking the peas," Evan said, arriving with a basket on his hip. He worked Sundays too, but he was off shift and shopping for his mother, which he kept announcing as though it embarrassed him. He leaned over Jacob's shoulder and squinted. "Why does your dot live outside the line?"

"That's the problem." Jacob tapped the curve with his pencil. "This is everything this country can make by itself. Every combination of fish and wool on the line or under it, they can have. Everything outside it, they can't. Not without something changing. But my answer key says that after they trade with the other country, they end up right here." He tapped the red dot. "Outside. Better than anything they could produce on their own, and the numbers aren't wrong. I've checked."

Evan pulled a bag of peas from under Jacob's elbow and dropped it in his basket. "So your answer key is wrong. That happens. Mr. Ruiz had a whole worksheet once where every answer was from the previous year's version."

"It's not wrong." Jacob said it with more certainty than he felt. He had the strange, specific sensation of standing at the edge of something he almost understood, the way he felt in geology class looking at a chunk of obsidian, all that igneous glass cooled from something that had once been liquid and moving. The idea was like that: fluid a second ago, hardening now. "The countries are different. One of them is better at fish, and even the one that's worse at everything still gives something up to make fish, and the trade price lands between what each of them gives up. So both of them end up with combinations they couldn't have made alone. That's the whole point. It's called comparative advantage." He heard himself say it and stopped, because Evan was staring at him. "I think," Jacob added.

"You think."

"I'm working on it."

Evan set his basket on the floor, which was against the rules, and crouched next to the frozen foods case. Somewhere behind them a compressor hummed; the cold coming off the case raised the hair on Jacob's arms. "Okay," Evan said. "Convince me with actual food. We're in a grocery store. Use the grocery store."

Jacob looked down the aisle. Coffee, tea, canned tomatoes, a pyramid of mandarin oranges in little mesh bags. He picked up two boxes of pasta, one in each hand, and held them out. "You're a country. I'm a country. Say I can make a lot of pasta and also canned tomatoes, and you can only make a little of either, but you're not quite as bad at tomatoes. If we each try to make both, we're both poorer than we have to be. If I make all the pasta and you make the tomatoes and we trade, we both end up with more of both than we started with. Both of us. The trade point is outside my curve because it's outside what I could do alone, not outside what we could do together."

"That sounds like a defense of plutocracy," Evan said. "One giant country owns all the pasta and everyone else has to take the deal."

"Maybe sometimes." Jacob put the boxes back, aligning them with the row. "That part I don't know yet. Ms. Dhillon said people malign the model for assuming things that aren't always true, that countries aren't really single things making single choices. I haven't figured out what I think about that." He looked at the red dot on his graph, outside the curve, and at the two boxes of pasta sitting in their ordinary row, and he understood that the sentence he would write tonight would be honest only if it said both things: the trade point was real, and so were the questions about it.

Evan picked up his basket. "Write the answer. Then tell me if you still believe it tomorrow."

Jacob gathered his papers. The cold had stiffened the top sheet, and his fingers were half numb as he squared the edges against the case. Behind him the freezer door swung shut, sealing the frost-white light inside, and he carried his graph down the aisle toward the registers, already composing the first sentence in his head.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Passover Seder, the youngest child able to do so traditionally asks the Four Questions, which begin 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
Grandmother Doris had run the Seder for forty years, and this year she was in a rehab facility learning to walk again, so the Haggadahs arrived at Justine's house in a cardboard box with a sticky note in her grandmother's handwriting: "The leader doesn't rush. That's the whole secret." Justine read it four times and then hid it in her pocket, because her mother had already cried twice that day and the note was not going to help.

She had led things before, sort of. Group projects, mostly, which mostly meant doing the work and letting Anita take credit for the presentation. This was different. Thirty-one relatives were coming, including her little cousin Benji, who was seven and had been practicing the Four Questions for three weeks with the desperate intensity of a boy who had already failed once. At the last Seder, two years ago, he had frozen at the word "dipping" and started to cry, and his mother had said, maybe unwisely, that it was fine, that they'd do it next year, and he had heard that as a verdict.

"He thinks he's broken now," Justine's older brother Danny told her while they arranged chairs. "Mom keeps saying he has nerves, like she's trying to pathologize a kid who just forgot a line."

"You could coach him. You did the questions for six years straight."

"I did my time," Danny said, and Justine understood, in a small cold way, that this was the year the job fell through the family like a coin through a grate, and she was standing where it landed.

The Seder began at sundown. Justine poured the first cup, said the Kiddush with her voice steadier than she'd expected, and made herself pause after each blessing the way the note said. The relatives noticed. Aunt Fern mouthed "who taught her that" across the table at Justine's mother, and Justine's mother, who had taught her nothing on purpose, pretended not to see.

Then came the problem. It was, of all things, the table. Benji was seated at the far end, wedged between two second cousins who were arguing about whether the afikoman had been hidden yet, and when Justine called for the questions, he stood up and his chair scraped and everyone turned and the room went quiet in that terrible way where you can hear the refrigerator. His mouth opened. Nothing came out.

Justine had planned for this, or half planned. She had thought about it in the shower that morning, weighing two instincts against each other: the instinct to save him, to have Danny start the first question and carry Benji along, which would be kind but would also tell Benji, again, that he couldn't; and the instinct to let him struggle, which felt like respecting him but might just be watching a kid drown in front of thirty people. She had not fully decided. She still hadn't. But she got up from her seat, walked the length of the table, and stood next to him.

"You start the whole thing with one sentence," she said, not quietly, so everyone heard. "Just the first one. Why is this night different."

"Why is this night," Benji said, "different from all other nights?"

"Perfect," Justine said, and the room exhaled, and Benji, gaining speed like a bike going downhill, asked all four questions straight through: why on this night they ate only matzah, why bitter herbs, why they dipped twice, why they reclined. Nobody at the table had heard the whole set from him before. Aunt Fern was actually dabbing her eyes, which Justine found both touching and a little profligate, given that there were still two hours of Seder to get through and probably only one tissue packet per aunt.

But leading was not one rescue, she discovered; it was arbitration, all night, between relatives with opinions. Great- Uncle Sol wanted the full Hebrew. Her mother wanted to skip a page to get to the food before the brisket dried out. Kayleigh, her friend from school who had come because her own family was out of town, sat next to Anita and whispered "wait, there's a sand witch?" when someone mentioned the orange on the seder plate, and Justine, who had not explained it well when she'd invited her, caught Kayleigh's eye and promised, silently, later.

Sol won the Hebrew, then lost the skipping argument when the brisket's fate became a matter of open floor debate. Justine ruled for the brisket. Sol called her "Judge" for the rest of the night, not entirely kindly, and poured himself a slightly larger glass of wine.

Near the end, after the third cup, her mother's phone lit up on the counter. It was Grandmother Doris, video calling from the facility. Justine carried the phone down the table and set it in the empty seat at the head, propped against a stack of Haggadahs, so that her grandmother could see the candles and the crumbs of matzah and Benji, who had by now sung "Chad Gadya" so many times he was hoarse. The screen showed a small, tired face in a hospital gown, in a room with fluorescent light, a hundred miles from the table she had built.

"You paused," her grandmother said. "I heard you pause."

"I rushed the Ten Plagues," Justine said.

"You rushed the Ten Plagues," her grandmother agreed. "You'll fix it next year."

The screen dimmed itself before Justine could ask whether next year meant her, whether the seat at the head was being passed or only loaned, and the question sat in her chest unfinished while everyone around her started stacking plates. Kayleigh tugged her sleeve and pointed at the orange. "Okay, but seriously," she said. "The sandwich thing. Tell me."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle in his 1704 book Opticks, an early version of the color wheel artists use today.
story:
Kyle had told everyone, twice, that he didn't care whether the painting got into the district show, and by the third time he said it he had almost convinced himself. He carried the canvas out to the backyard anyway, setting it on the old picnic table beside the tubs of paint, because the light there was better in the afternoon and because the kitchen table was covered with his brother's college forms and his mother kept asking questions about colors through the window. He wanted to finish the painting today. That was the only reason he'd refused Arnav's invitation to the lake, and the fact that he'd made up an excuse about a dentist appointment instead of saying so was not something he planned to examine.

The painting was of the backyard itself, the fence, the leaning maple, the wheelbarrow his father never emptied. He had gotten as far as the tree when the trouble started. The greens were off. Every green he mixed looked either like toothpaste or like something that had died in a fridge, and the more he layered, the worse it got. He sat back, pressed his thumb into the paint on the palette, and admitted to himself that he had no idea what he was doing. Then he corrected that thought: he had some idea. He had watched videos. He had opinions. He simply had no system.

Arnav came through the gate at four, still holding the lake towel, because Arnav never accepted a dentist excuse at face value. "You're hiding," Arnav said. "You're hiding in your own yard, which is a new low." Kyle said he wasn't hiding, he was working, which was true, and also a dodge, since the two could coexist. Arnav dropped the towel on the grass, picked up the palette knife, and turned it over like evidence. "It looks like the tree is sick," he said. "Like it's asking to be put down."

Kyle started to defend the greens, heard how petulant his own voice went in his head, and stopped. "The problem isn't the green," he said. "The problem is everything around it. It's all the same temperature. Nothing pushes against anything." Arnav asked what that meant, pushing, and Kyle realized he couldn't quite say. He knew it when he saw it in other paintings, the way a small patch of red made a green field suddenly alive, but he'd been treating color like an ingredient list instead of a set of relationships.

Mr. Ngo, the neighbour, was watering his tomatoes along the fence, and had been listening in the way he listened, without pretending not to. "You're circling something," he said over the water. "You know what you're missing has a shape." Kyle laughed at that, because it sounded like a fortune cookie, but later, scrubbing brushes, the shape became literal. Circle. His art teacher freshman year had drawn one on the board, a ring of colors, red opposite green, and he'd copied it into a notebook he no longer had. He tried to reconstruct it from memory, smearing dots of paint on a scrap of board, ordering them the way a rainbow ordered itself, and looping the ends together.

Arnav, who read the strangest things, looked over his shoulder and frowned. "That's Newton," Arnav said. "Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle." Kyle said no, that was an art thing, invented by some painter. Arnav pulled out his phone, then turned it toward him: Newton, in his 1704 book Opticks, had bent the spectrum into a circle, and artists' color wheels came down from that. Kyle read the screen twice. A physicist. The tool every artist he'd ever studied leaned on had started with a man thinking about light, not about paint. It was like finding out the alphabet had been designed by a mathematician.

He tried the wheel's logic on the canvas. Green, opposed by red. He mixed a dull brick red, thinned it, and dragged it through the shadow side of the maple's foliage, and the green went from toothpaste to leaf without him touching the green at all. He worked fast while the light lasted, laying the red into the fence shadows too, until the yard on the canvas had the consonance the real yard had always had and his painting had lacked, everything held together by what opposed it. It was a small thing, a correction, not a transformation. He would not have admitted, before, that a problem could be solved by adding what didn't belong.

Arnav stood beside him, arms folded, studying it. "So are you entering it or not?" Kyle said he hadn't decided, which was the same lie in a cleaner shirt. Arnav waited. Kyle picked up the brush, touched red to the corner of the wheelbarrow, and said, "Ask me when it's dry."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Near Earth's surface a projectile's vertical velocity changes by about 9.8 metres per second every second, whether it is rising or falling.
story:
The ball rose, hung, and fell, and Hailey counted under her breath until it struck the launch pad again. "One point nine seconds," she said, thumbing the stopwatch on the tablet beside the exhibit. The machine at the science museum fired its small silver ball straight up every fifteen seconds, and she had now timed it four times.

"You're going to lambaste yourself if you keep staring at that thing," Dario said. "We're supposed to be finding the friction exhibit for the write-up. Kayden's already texting me about it."

"One more." She reset the watch. The next ball went up, and she counted again, and this time she also watched the little digital readout on the console, the one that flashed the vertical speed as the ball climbed. Thirty kilometers per hour. Twenty. Ten. Then the numbers reversed on the way down, climbing back the same steps they had come down. She copied the column into her notebook.

"There's something wrong with the machine," she said when Dario came back across the hall. "It slows down going up, fine, that makes sense, I guess. But it speeds up coming down at exactly the same rate. The numbers match. Every step."

Dario leaned over her notebook. "So?"

"So it's weird. I thought falling was different. Heavier, faster, something." She tapped the column. "It goes from ten to twenty to thirty on the way down, same as it went from thirty to ten on the way up. Turned around, like a mirror."

Kayden arrived with two paper cones from the water dispenser and a look of incipient rebellion. "Ms. Rahman says we're behind. Both of you. She's by the pendulum."

At the pendulum, Ms. Rahman did not lecture, which Hailey had learned was her way of being severe. She only asked what they had found. Dario showed the friction exhibit, half finished. Hailey, before she could decide not to, turned her notebook around and said the machine's ball slowed on the way up and sped up on the way down, and the rate was the same both ways.

"Then that's your write-up," Ms. Rahman said. "Time the flight. You have the total. What can you do with it?"

Hailey stood very still. The total time, one point nine seconds, meant the ball spent half of that rising and half falling. She remembered the Tuesday problem set, the one she'd copied the method for without trusting it: you split the motion. Sideways and up-down, separate, like keeping two bank accounts for the same paycheck. "If I knew how fast the vertical speed changes each second," she said slowly, "I could work backwards to the launch speed."

At home that night she cleared the hallway between the kitchen door and the coat hooks, took the tennis ball from the garage, and asked her mother to time her throws on her phone. Her mother obliged with the weary efficiency of someone who had survived Hailey's rock collection and her telescope phase. The first throw was crooked and clipped the light fixture, and her mother said one word, the name of a lamp, in a tone Hailey chose to hear as encouragement. The second throw went up clean. Two seconds, roughly. She tried softer, harder, watched the ball's sluggishness at the top, the gathering speed below it, and wrote the numbers down.

At school the next morning she found Dario at the lab table before class. "Here's my syllogism," she said. "The ball's vertical speed changes by the same amount each second going up and coming down. The machine and my hallway both say so. So if I split any throw into sideways and up-down parts, the up-down part alone tells me the height and the hang time, and the sideways part is just steady the whole way. Two separate problems wearing one ball."

"That's not really a syllogism," Dario said. "That's more of a method."

"It's a syllogism if I want it to be." She slid the notebook across. "The machine's readout, my mom's timing, and the Tuesday problems all agree. But I still don't get why the rate is the same both directions. It just is, as far as anything in my notebook says. That part I'm leaving blank."

Kayden leaned over from the next table. "Ms. Rahman's coming."

Hailey flipped the notebook open to the clean page and drew a ball, an arrow up, an arrow sideways, and beneath them, in small letters, the rate she had measured: near the ground, about 9.8 metres per second of change, every second, rising or falling. She squared the page flat with her palm and pushed her pen behind her ear as Ms. Rahman's shadow crossed the table.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: French engineer Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone.
story:
Savannah found the rope coiled beside the kickboard bin on the first Tuesday of dryland training, and Ms. Pritchard stood over it with a stopwatch and the particular patience of someone who had decided something. The team sat on the pool deck in their suits, dripping, twelve of them counting down the weeks to regionals. Carlo, who had opinions about everything except his own backstroke, leaned toward Savannah and said, "If she makes us pull that thing, I'm abrogating my contract." He had no contract. He had never had a contract. It was a running joke from the autumn, when the school had made everyone sign a behaviour agreement and he had read his aloud in a French accent until Ms. Pritchard confiscated it.

"I need eight of you on this rope," she said. "The rest hold the erg strap. We're testing something." Savannah took a place near the middle, third from the front, where effort was hardest to see. Annabella stood behind her and whispered that the rope smelled like the bottom of a gym bag, which was accurate, and somehow made the whole exercise feel like antiquity, something gladiators might have done before the bread and the circuses. They pulled when the whistle went. The rope creaked, the knot groaned against the cleat, and the load, a weighted sled on the tile runner, moved exactly nowhere for three full seconds.

Afterward Ms. Pritchard called each of them aside one at a time to pull alone, the same sled, the same rope, and Savannah watched the numbers on the spring scale clipped to the line. Carlo, who had spent the group pull giggling, put up a mark that was frankly startling. Annabella, quiet and diligent, nearly matched him. Every single one of them, alone, pulled harder than they had together, and Savannah stood at the end of the lane with a towel around her neck doing the arithmetic twice, because it seemed like a thing someone should double-check. At home that night she looked it up and found him, a French engineer named Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, who had found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone. She read it three times. There was no reason given, just the finding, sitting there like a coin found in a drain.

She thought about the medley relay, about how she swam her anchor leg a shade easier when the team was far behind, a shade she had never admitted to herself until now. It was easier to be carried by a loss than to fight a losing one alone.

Carlo's side of the week was simpler and more complicated. He had decided, standing alone at the rope with everyone watching, that he would rather be seen trying and failing than trying and succeeding, because succeeding alone meant he had no excuse for the rest of the season. When Ms. Pritchard showed him his number, he laughed and said, "So Ringelmann says I'm a fraud," and she said only, "Ringelmann says you pull harder alone," which was not the same sentence, though Carlo did not notice the difference at first. He noticed it later, in the shower, and it bothered him through his whole sandwich at lunch.

On Thursday Ms. Pritchard changed the arrangement. She split them into pairs, one on the rope and one watching the scale, and made them trade. "Call the number out," she said. "Every pull, out loud." The deck got loud fast. Annabella, who had assumed she was the weakest on the team, turned out to hold her number almost perfectly, group or alone, and she went very pink when Carlo shouted her score across the pool like a race caller at a county fair. "Annabella Kowalski, untouched by Ringelmann, ladies and gentlemen, a machine of antiquity," he bellowed, and got a kickboard thrown at his head, and everyone laughed, even Ms. Pritchard, briefly.

Savannah stood at the scale for Carlo's pull and watched the needle tremble up and hold. It held. Then she took the rope herself and heard him call her number, and it was lower than her solo mark from Tuesday, and she heard it, out loud, in her own ears, and pulled harder until the needle climbed. She found she could do that. Not dramatically, not like a movie, just a few pounds of difference that nobody watching would see, but that she could feel in her forearms like a correction of the record.

The twist arrived on Friday, and it belonged to Annabella. She asked Ms. Pritchard whether the whole thing meant they should all just train alone, since together was apparently a scam, and the putative lesson of the week collapsed the moment she said it, because Ms. Pritchard said, "No, it means watch each other," and pointed at the relay result from Saturday, which none of them had thought to connect: their four times, added up, were faster than any of them had gone individually all season. Savannah sat with that on the bus home, the two findings side by side and refusing to agree, ropes and relays, less and more, and she did not try to force them into one neat sentence.

At regionals she stood on the blocks for her anchor leg with the team four tenths behind. She thought of the needle trembling, of Carlo shouting, of Ringelmann in 1913 with his rope, and then she stopped thinking and dove.

"Twelve pounds more than Tuesday," Carlo said afterward, holding up the stopwatch like a subpoena. "I did the math."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Pomp and Circumstance became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music.
story:
Peyton had the living room to herself, which meant the flute came out. She stood by the window with the music stand her mother used for recipes and played the trio from Pomp and Circumstance for the ninth time that afternoon, stopping at the same place each time, where the clarinets came in and she had to imagine them. Outside, a neighbour was washing a car that was already clean.

Her cap and gown hung on the closet door, still in their plastic, and beneath them, on the desk, sat a printout of the graduation program. Her name was in it twice. Once in the long alphabetical list, and once near the bottom, under the heading that read "Senior Address: Peyton Okafor." She had written three drafts of the speech, and all three of them were terrible in different ways, and the ceremony was in two days.

Elissa came over around four, letting herself in through the back door the way she had since they were nine. She dropped onto the couch with her phone already in her hand. "Harry says rehearsal ran late because the trumpets can't count rests. He counted for them. Out loud. Mr. Duarte moved him to the back row."

"He's still coming Sunday?"

"He's bringing his whole family, I think. Grandparents, an aunt, possibly a cousin nobody's met." Elissa looked up. "Play the march again. The middle part."

Peyton played it. When she finished, Elissa said, "You know what I never thought about until this week? Why it's that song. Every graduation in every movie, every actual graduation, always the same one. Nobody ever votes on it. It just is."

"I looked it up." Peyton set the flute on the stand. "It's because of Yale. In 1905 they played it at their commencement, and Elgar got an honorary doctorate of music there, and after that it just spread. Every school copied them." She said this with the flatness of someone reciting something she had read twice to be sure. "Nineteen-oh-five. That's the whole reason."

"Huh." Elissa considered it. "So some college band played a march once and now my grandmother will cry to it on Sunday without knowing why."

"Basically."

"That's either beautiful or really stupid."

Peyton sat down on the arm of the couch. That was the exact fork she had been standing at for two days, though she hadn't put it in those words. The first draft of her speech had been about tradition, the weight of it, the long chain of people who had worn the same polyester gown. It had calcified somewhere around the second page and turned into a museum plaque. The second draft had been an attack on ritual, all of it, caps and cords and the march itself, and she had read it out loud and heard her own voice doing something performative and thin. The third draft she had written in a kind of ascetic mood, stripped down to plain sentences, and it was honest but it said nothing, like a room with the furniture removed.

"Here's my problem," she said. "Half of me thinks the copying is the point. Like, everyone who ever graduated stood up when that music played, and now I do too, and that's the only version of belonging that isn't fake. And the other half thinks it's just a habit nobody's questioned in a hundred and twenty years, and treating a habit like it's sacred is a kind of subterfuge. You're pretending the boring thing is profound so you don't have to admit it's boring."

"Which half wrote the current draft?"

"Neither. There is no current draft. There's a document with my name on it and a blinking cursor."

Elissa laughed, then stopped laughing, which was worse. "You could just say the true thing. Whatever the true thing actually is."

"The true thing is I don't know which half is right. I keep thinking I've decided and then I play the march and it gets me, and I'm furious that it gets me, because it's a piece of background music for a ceremony about myself and it still gets me."

Ms. Horváth, who had retired to the house next door two years ago and could be relied upon to know everything happening within a three-block radius, appeared at the back door with a plate of lemon squares, which she handed over on the understanding that Peyton's mother would return the plate washed. She stayed for ten minutes, mostly to complain about the school board's parking plan for Sunday, and on her way out she paused at the music stand.

"You're the one playing the solo?" she asked. Peyton nodded. Ms. Horváth looked at the sheet music for a moment as if reading it. "My husband marched to that at City College in 1968. He said half the row was thinking about Vietnam and the other half was thinking about lunch, and the music didn't care. It just kept going." She let herself out.

Elissa raised her eyebrows. Peyton picked the flute back up, and this time she played the trio all the way through, past where the clarinets would have come in, into the passage that repeated and lifted and repeated again, the part everyone in the audience would be humming without knowing where they'd learned it. When she lowered the flute, Elissa was quiet for a second.

"So what are you going to tell two hundred people in folding chairs?"

Peyton looked at the printout on the desk, at her own name sitting there small and ordinary in eleven-point font. She went and got her laptop and opened the document with the blinking cursor and typed one sentence, then deleted it, then typed it again and left it.

"Okay," she said. "Now play the part with the trumpets."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Under US law, an artwork is protected by copyright automatically the moment it is created in a fixed form; registration is voluntary, though needed before suing over a US work.
story:
The printmaking shack at Camp Wren smelled of ink and pine sap, and Alexia had claimed the corner table by the window on the first day. Now, three weeks into the session, ten test prints hung above her like moths pinned to cork: each one a variation on the same subject, her grandmother's hands, drawn from memory and from a single photograph she kept folded in her sketchbook. The assignment from Mr. Islam was to build a portfolio of ten artworks around one theme and write an artist's statement to hold it together, and the theme she had chosen was turning out to be harder than she'd expected. It kept sliding between memory and evidence, between what she remembered and what the photograph could prove.

"You should see Douglas's statement," Tatum said, dropping onto the stool beside her. "Two paragraphs on water as a metaphor. Mine's about doors, which sounded deep in June and now sounds like a hardware catalogue."

Alexia smoothed a print flat with the heel of her hand. "Mine keeps turning into a eulogy. I don't want it to be a eulogy. She's still alive. She just doesn't remember the garden anymore."

"That's the theme, though. Hands that built something they can't find anymore."

Outside, the lake lay flat and white under the afternoon glare. Tatum leaned over the sketchbook and flipped to the photograph without asking, which Alexia disliked and allowed, because Tatum had known her grandmother too, back when the garden still had a fence and the fence still had a gate.

"Are you going to post them when you get home? The whole set?"

Alexia hadn't decided. She'd been avoiding the question all week, the way she avoided the photograph's back, where her grandmother had written a date and nothing else. She had an account on a portfolio site, half-built, four old drawings of barns she no longer cared about. Ten new pieces, her best work, put where anyone with a browser could save them, print them, take them.

"If I post them, anyone can just use them," she said. "Right? Like, that's what my mom says about everything. Once it's on the internet it belongs to everyone."

"That's not actually true," Tatum said. "My cousin does graphic design. She told me once you make something, it's protected. Like, automatically."

"Automatically how?"

"Copyright. It exists the second it's, like, fixed. The moment it's made in a fixed form, it's protected. She said registration is voluntary, but you'd need it before you could sue anyone over a US work." Tatum said it fast, the way she recited things she'd heard once and half-stored. "She made me memorize it because I posted her flyers once without asking."

Alexia turned that over while she cleaned the brayer with a rag gone black at the folds. The ink coagulate on the roller had to be worked off in small circles or it would dry into the texture and ruin the next pass, and she did the small circles and thought about fixed form. A print was about as fixed as anything got. Ink pressed into damp paper. The protection, apparently, was already there, clinging to the work the way the ink clung, without her doing anything, without a form or a fee or a stamp from some office. Registration was voluntary, an option held in reserve, something you'd need only if it came to a fight over a US work. She found the distinction quietly steadying: the art was hers by the fact of its making, and what came after was choice.

"So posting them doesn't give them away," she said.

"Gives them away less than keeping them in a drawer," Tatum said. "Nobody can steal what nobody sees. My cousin also says that, but I think she made it up."

Mr. Islam came through on his rounds, hands clasped behind him, and stopped at her wall of hands. He looked for a long time. "The third one," he said finally. "You've been holding back on the third one. It's the only one where you stopped being polite."

She didn't know what he meant until that evening, when she sat with the statement draft under the porch light and read the third print again. It was the roughest, the ink too heavy, the knuckles blurred. She had made it the night her mother called to say the garden gate had been left open all winter and no one had noticed. It was the only print she'd thought was a failure, and it was the only one that told the truth: that the loss was already underway, that memory was not a genealogy passed cleanly down but a thing with gaps, missing links, whole branches gone dark. Her statement had been trying to apologize for that print. She crossed out two paragraphs and started over with a single sentence: my grandmother's hands built a garden she can no longer find, and I am trying to hold what remains.

The next morning she photographed all ten pieces in the flat light off the lake, laying them on the dock one at a time. Douglas wandered over mid-way, holding a mug of something herbal he'd been drinking all week to demonstrate discipline.

"You're posting before camp ends?" he asked.

"After I finish the statement." She squared the fourth print against the dock boards. "It's protected anyway, the moment it's fixed. It's a print, it doesn't get more fixed."

"What if someone uses them anyway?"

"Then registering is voluntary but it's there if I need it before suing. Over a US work," she said, and heard Tatum's cadence in her own voice, and laughed at herself. "I'm not going to sue a stranger over my grandmother's hands. I just wanted to know the ground was solid before I stood on it."

She was still uncertain, and she was honest with herself about where. The protection existed, but she couldn't shake the feeling that the internet was a country with different weather, where the rules held loosely and people took things anyway. She would post nine of the ten. The third one, the one where she'd stopped being polite, she would keep in the flat portfolio case, shown to teachers and admissions readers only, because some truths she wanted witnessed, not scattered. That was a position she could hold, assembled from two ways of thinking, the law's calm guarantee and her own stubborn care, and she knew it might change by winter.

At the last campfire, Tatum nudged her with an elbow. "Did you post them?"

"Nine. The tenth one's mine for now."

"Which one?"

"The failure," Alexia said, and pulled her jacket tighter as the smoke drifted toward the water.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A security deposit is held to cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear, so in many jurisdictions a landlord cannot deduct for ordinary aging like small nail holes.
story:
The key to his grandfather's garden flat was warm from Sebastian's pocket by the time he reached the gate. Ms. Han had left it in the mailbox with a note: "Last boxes Saturday. Thank you for the two years." His grandfather had put the whole matter in Sebastian's hands with an air of ceremony, as though transferring something more than a chore. "Inspect everything," he had said. "The deposit is fifteen hundred. She was a good tenant, but walls get ruined, and I still owe the bank on this house for another eleven years. The mortgage doesn't pause because someone was polite."

Sebastian had nodded at the time, though the numbers had startled him. He knew his grandfather had bought the house decades ago with a down payment scraped together from two jobs, and that the small flat over the garage now paid most of the monthly instalment. Rent in, mortgage out; the house, in a sense, lived off itself. What Sebastian had not known, until he started reading that week instead of studying for chemistry, was what a security deposit was actually for. He had assumed it belonged to the landlord, a kind of trophy held against bad behaviour. The tenancy website his classmate Estelle sent him said otherwise, in a paragraph he had read four times while the rain made an interminable drumming on his window.

Estelle arrived at nine with her mother's van and her own agenda, which she announced before she had even closed the door. "I want this flat," she said. "For first year, if I go to the university here. My parents said if I can cover rent from the bursary and my job, I can live out of the dorms." She looked around the empty rooms the way other people looked at ocean. "So whatever happens with the deposit, do it fairly, because I have to live with your grandfather after."

"Your erudition is showing," Sebastian said, and she stuck her tongue out at him, but she was right to say it, and they both knew it. He began at the front wall with his phone. He photographed every surface, every corner, the skirting boards, the inside of the cupboards, the ceiling where a pipe had once wept and been fixed. Ms. Han appeared in the doorway carrying a lamp she had missed, watched him work for a moment, and said nothing. She was a retired music teacher, small and precise, and Sebastian had liked her since she had complimented his terrible recorder playing at age nine with a completely straight face.

There were nail holes. Small ones, a scatter of them above the mantel where she had hung, he remembered, a row of framed photographs of orchestras. There was a scuff on the kitchen doorframe and a pale rectangle on the bedroom wall where a poster had kept the paint from fading. His grandfather, arriving at eleven with a folded newspaper under his arm, stood in front of the mantel and tapped it. "Fill and paint, that's a day's work and materials. I'll take it out of the deposit."

"That's ordinary wear and tear," Sebastian said. He had practised not saying it like a speech. "Nail holes, small ones. It's what the deposit is for, but only the other things. It's held to cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear, not the way a place just ages when someone lives in it properly." His grandfather's face did something complicated. Ms. Han, who had been lifting a box of sheet music, set it down slowly.

"George told me landlords always keep something," she said, naming her son, who lived abroad and phoned her on Sundays full of advice. "He said that's just how it is." Sebastian showed them both the photographs on his phone, the holes like faint stars above the mantel, and then the website, and his grandfather read the paragraph twice with his glasses pushed up on his forehead, his mouth working as though chewing something difficult. The house had cost him his thirties; that was true and could not be refunded either.

"You'll want the whole fifteen hundred for textbooks," he said finally to Ms. Han, "so let's not argue." Then, to Sebastian, quieter, almost grudging: "The scuff, though. That I'll paint myself." It was as close as he came to admitting anything, and Sebastian understood that the admission was not really about paint. His grandfather had spent a lifetime believing that ownership was a series of small defences, that a house had to be indemnified against everyone who passed through it. It had perhaps not occurred to him that a tenant could leave a place better defended than the landlord himself.

Ms. Han transferred the money right there, standing in the empty living room, and then handed Estelle a key of her own accord, saying the water heater needed two minutes and the radiator in the back room never quite warmed the corner by the window. Estelle held the key in both hands like a bird. Sebastian went on photographing the walls anyway, finishing what he had started, until his grandfather put a hand on his shoulder and steered him toward the gate. "Lock up behind us," his grandfather said, "and leave the latch off. She still has the lamp."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: In Chicago, MLA and APA styles, entries in the final list of sources are arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited.
story:
The paper was due at midnight and Hannah's bibliography ran in the order she had used the sources, De Beauvoir third because she had read her third, halfway through the draft on a Tuesday. She attached the file at eleven forty, then sat with her laptop open on her bed, thumbing the edge of the trackpad, and did not send it.

Mr. Watanabe had assigned it in September: eight pages, a real argument, footnotes, and a bibliography in a standard style, which Hannah had chosen from a handout the way you choose a lottery number. "Pick one and be consistent," he had said, and she had picked MLA because it was first alphabetically on the list, which she now suspected was the only kind of alphabetizing she had ever actually done.

She texted Jaxson at eleven forty-three. He answered with a question mark, which in their shorthand meant come over or stop being dramatic, depending. She chose come over, and he was on her front step twelve minutes later in his work shirt from the grocery store, smelling faintly of the floral aisle, a florid pink receipt still in his jacket pocket from the girl he would not name.

"Show me," he said.

She turned the laptop toward him. He scrolled to the end, past the argument about whether beauty standards could be both culturally constructed and personally sincere, past the footnote she was proud of, and stopped at the works cited page. He was quiet long enough that she started defending herself.

"I did the citations right. I checked."

"That's not it." He tapped the screen. "It's the order."

"What's wrong with the order?"

"You listed them in the order you used them."

She stared at the page. De Beauvoir sat fourth from the top, above Wolf, below hooks, a small chronicle of her reading habits laid out for Mr. Watanabe to grade. In September, in the first week of class, she had watched Mr. Watanabe hand back a sample paper from some former student and hold it up without comment, and she had thought the lesson was about the thesis. Now she thought it might have been about the last page, which she had not even looked at, because who looks at the last page of a sample.

"So what order is it," she said.

Jaxson pulled up something on his phone, a university page with a chart, and turned it around. She read it twice. In Chicago, MLA and APA, entries in the final list of sources were arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited. Not the order cited. Not the order she had bled through at two in the morning, three weeks of reading compressed into a sequence that she had assumed mattered because it had mattered to her.

"Why would they not care about the order you used them?"

"Not my problem," Jaxson said. "Eleven fifty-one."

She began to retype, dragging entries into their new arrangement, and the page reorganized itself into something she had not planned: all the A's at the top, strangers to each other, a sociologist beside a novelist beside a magazine piece she had found on the last day and almost not used. It looked, she thought, like a party where everyone had been seated by something other than friendship. She kept working and did not say this out loud.

There was a knock at the door at eleven fifty-four, soft, and Oceanne let herself in with the spare key Hannah's mother had given her in eleventh grade for reasons neither of them could now reconstruct. She had a thermos and the expression she wore when she intended to be difficult. "You're not seriously doing this tonight."

"She has four minutes," Jaxson said.

"He said midnight." Oceanne dropped onto the couch. "He also said the grade is ten percent of the semester. One point for a bibliography order. Send it as is."

It was not one point, probably. It was Mr. Watanabe, who had once kept a homework assignment she turned in with the margins wrong, and had written only "Again" at the top, and she had done it again, correctly, hating him a little, and had never gotten that assignment back wrong since. Oceanne's way was speed and survival. Jaxson's was that rules existed and you followed them or you didn't, there was nothing to discuss. Hannah sat between the two of them on the couch with her cursor blinking in the middle of a half-alphabetized page.

"It's not about the one point," she said.

"Then what's it about?"

She couldn't say it cleanly. Something about how she had written the paper, how De Beauvoir had come to her third because Oceanne had said read the fiction first, and now the paper would say nothing about that, would present her thinking as a neat alphabet as if she had always known where she was going, which she hadn't. But the citation said what it said. The arrangement was alphabetical by surname in all three of the styles, so the choice of style hadn't even saved her, and the honesty she wanted the page to carry was apparently not something a bibliography was built to carry. She finished moving the last entry at eleven fifty-eight.

"Send it," Jaxson said.

"Leave it a day," Oceanne said. "Email him, tell him you caught something."

Hannah looked at the screen, the cursor resting at the end of the final line, the sources standing in their new order like people who had agreed to be sorted by something indifferent to how they had actually met her.

"One minute," Jaxson said.

She moved the cursor to the submit button and left it there.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A getter that returns a reference to a private mutable object, such as a list, lets outside code change it, so programmers often return a copy instead.
story:
The coding club met on Thursdays in the back lab of the science wing, where the radiators clanked and nobody bothered to fix the projector. Maika arrived early to claim the machine by the window, because that one still ran the IDE without wheezing. She had spent the week deciding what to build: a small program called ReadingLog that would hold her books, her ratings, one sentence about each. Her plan for the afternoon was narrower than that. She wanted a class with private fields, the way Ms. Bouchard had written on the board in October, private meaning that only the class itself could touch what was inside.

She typed the field first, a private ArrayList of strings, then the constructor, then a getter named getBooks that returned the list. It compiled on the first try, which felt like a small gift. She wrote a test in a second file, asked the object for its list, and printed the size. Three. Correct. She sat back with the flat satisfaction of a checkpoint reached.

Marcel dropped into the chair beside her with the sound of someone arriving late on purpose. He had a folder open on his laptop full of screenshots, a mockup of an app he called StudyStreak, which he intended, he said, to monetize by the end of the school year. He wanted Maika's ReadingLog class as the engine, something his users could fill with their own lists, something solid with her name on the commit history. "Your code is clean," he said, which from Marcel was both a compliment and a request. Joey leaned over from the next row and said it was definitely going to blow up, definitely, and Maika watched Marcel absorb the praise without examining it, the way he never examined Joey's opinion of anything.

"I need to try breaking it first," she said. "Give me ten minutes."

Marcel, sanguine about all timelines including hers, shrugged and went back to his mockup. Ms. Bouchard circled the room with her coffee, pausing at each screen long enough to make people straighten up, but she never read over anyone's shoulder for more than a sentence, which was a kindness Maika had come to appreciate. When she reached Maika, she only said, "Watch what your test can reach," and moved on.

In the test file, then in a third class Marcel had pasted in to simulate his app, Maika wrote a few lines. She called getBooks on her object, held the list it gave back, and called clear on it from outside the class. Then she asked the object for its size. The console printed zero. Her three books, her ratings, her one careful sentence about the novel she had finished at two in the morning, all gone, and the class had never once complained, because nothing private had technically been touched. The getter had handed out a reference, the same list, the actual one, and outside code could change it through that door.

She stared at the zero for a while. It was not a crash, which was somehow worse; a crash at least announced itself. She thought of her mother's kitchen drawer of duplicates, spare keys cut for neighbours over the years, and how you could not call a house private once four families could open it. Then she thought of Marcel's users, hundreds of imaginary strangers, one of them bound to clear a list either by accident or on purpose, and StudyStreak quietly losing everything. She fixed it without announcing the fix: getBooks now built a new list, copied the entries in, and returned the copy. She tested it again, clearing what came back, and the object still held three. The original stayed hers.

"Done," she said, and turned her screen so Marcel could see the class. He read it fast, then slower, and she watched him find the line where the copy was made. He did not say anything clever for once. "Why the new list?" he asked, and she said, "Because a getter that returns the list itself lets anyone change it. So I return a copy." He was quiet, tapping one finger on the table edge, and she understood that his silence was the sound of him thinking about his users, or his revenue, or both, and that these were not the same thing but could still point in the same direction.

"You could charge for that," Joey offered from the next row, and Marcel told him to can it, though not unkindly. He copied the class into his project and credited her in the comment at the top, her full name spelled right. There was still a question Maika could not close, though, and she kept it to herself for the moment: whether a copy every time would make Marcel's app slow once the lists grew long, whether there was a way to be both safe and quick, and whether she would know enough by the end of term to judge. She wrote the question on a sticky note and pressed it to the bottom of her screen, next to the one that said radiator, third Thursday, bring gloves.
