Ms. Bouchard passed behind them on her last loop, paused at the test results still open on Maika's monitor, the run showing zero and then three, and set a wrapped mint beside the keyboard without a word. Maika pocketed it and started typing the next test.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 13 in 100 people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy, mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time.
story:
The pamphlet in Tyler's hand had a cartoon condom on the front, wearing what appeared to be sunglasses, and he thought about throwing it in the wastebasket beside the coffee machine. Instead he folded it into quarters and put it in his jacket, because in eleven days he was supposed to stand in front of a dormitory lounge full of freshmen and say words out loud, and he had promised Mr. Swampy he would come to the clinic first.

"You're sweating," Laurence said from the chair beside him. "It's a doctor's office, not an execution."

"It's a rehearsal. That's worse."

Mr. Swampy's door opened and a nurse beckoned them in. The room smelled of alcohol wipes and paper. There was a plastic model of a pelvis on the counter that Tyler tried very hard not to look at, and a whiteboard on which someone had drawn a stick figure holding a sign that read ASK ME ANYTHING.

"All right," Mr. Swampy said, pulling over a stool. "You're my peer health educator for the fall, which means in twenty minutes I need to believe you can actually educate. Laurence, you play the skeptical freshman. Tyler, go."

Laurence slouched against the wall in an impression of boredom so precise it was almost insulting. "Okay, so," Tyler began, "condoms. They're, uh, on the shelf at any drugstore, they're cheap, and they work." He heard the words land flat, like a dropped tray.

"Work how?" Laurence said. "My cousin said the box says ninety-eight percent. That's basically perfect, right? Like, why would anyone bother with anything else."

Tyler's mouth opened and nothing came out. He looked at the whiteboard, the pelvis, the pamphlet's edge poking out of his jacket. The ninety-eight number was on the box, he knew that much, and yet something in the back of his mind from the training manual kept knocking. He pulled the pamphlet out and unfolded it, and there it was, the sentence he'd skimmed and then, stupidly, skipped. "It says here," he said slowly, "that with typical use, about thirteen in a hundred people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy." He read it twice more, the second time silently, because he did not want to get it wrong. "So the box number is one thing. Real life is another."

Laurence had stopped slouching. "Thirteen out of a hundred? That's way more than two."

"Yeah." Tyler turned the pamphlet toward him. "Mostly because they're not used correctly every time." He looked up at Mr. Swampy, expecting to be corrected, and found the doctor nodding once, arms folded, giving nothing away. "So the honest answer isn't 'condoms are basically perfect.' It's more like, use one, use it right, every time, and know that it's still smart to think about a second method."

"Huh," said Laurence, in the tone he reserved for things that had actually surprised him.

Mr. Swampy erased the stick figure and wrote TESTED across the board. "Next section. You're talking to someone who's scared to walk into this building. What do you say?"

Tyler took a breath. He'd practiced this part in his bedroom until his mother banged on the wall, and it still felt like stepping off a curb in the dark. "I'd say it's confidential. You don't need a parent, you can ask for the costs up front, and the actual appointment is fast. They ask you questions, they take a sample, urine or a swab depending on what they're testing for, and a lot of it you can do without an exam at all." He paused. "And I'd say that asking to be tested doesn't mean anything about who you are. It means you decided to know."

"And consent?" Mr. Swampy said. "That's the one they'll push back on."

"That it's not a contract you sign once." The words came easier now, maybe because he'd finally said the other numbers out loud first. "It's something you check on, every time, and either person can change their mind. If someone's too drunk or too scared to answer, that's not a yes. If they go quiet, that's not a yes. You ask, and you listen for the actual answer."

Kristen appeared in the doorway holding two sodas from the machine, having bailed on the last ten minutes of her own rehearsal to get drinks for everyone. "Am I late for the part where he bombs?"

"He didn't bomb," Laurence said. "He found out the box is lying and told me anyway. I thought he was going to be one of those ideologues about it, all purity and pamphlets. Like it's a religion and he's the ascetic monk of the health office."

Tyler laughed, and something in his chest that had been clenched since the waiting room let go. "I got the number wrong an hour ago," he admitted. "I would have told them ninety-eight and sent them home."

Mr. Swampy capped his pen. "Which is why we rehearse. You'll get things wrong in that lounge too. What matters is that you correct it in front of them when you do."

"Can you come the first night?" Tyler asked Laurence. "Sit in the back and be the annoying one?"

Laurence cracked his soda. "Only if I get to ask about the thirteen again."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Kahlo's The Broken Column (1944), her spine is painted as a cracked Ionic column visible through an opening in her body.
story:
The print of The Broken Column had been taped above the whiteboard since September, and Julia had stopped seeing it weeks ago, the way you stop seeing a fire exit sign. Now Mr. Bianchi had assigned each of them a painting to critique, formal analysis only, and she had drawn Kahlo's name from the envelope he held open at the door. "Lucky," Bryson whispered behind her, and she wasn't sure whether he meant it or was being kind, because Bryson said most things in a voice that could go either way.

She stayed after the bell to look properly. The room smelled of turpentine from third period, and the janitor's cart rattled somewhere down the hall. Up close the painting refused to behave. The figure stood in a desert, a green landscape split by a chasm, and down the middle of her body ran a tear, an opening in the skin, and inside the opening was a column. Julia leaned forward until her breath fogged the projector screen.

"Why is there architecture in her chest," she said, not quite a question, and Ali, who had stayed to finish a charcoal sketch and pretended not to be listening, looked up.

"It's her spine," Ali said. "It's a cracked Ionic column, through the opening in her body." She turned back to her sketch, then added, "Ionic's the one with the scrolls on top. I looked it up last night, for fun." She said "for fun" the way people apologize for caring about something.

Julia wrote it down. Then she wrote, in the margin, that she didn't know yet what to do with it. Her first instinct was the essay she could write in her sleep: the column as symbol of ruin, the body as a building that had failed, pain made classical and therefore dignified. It would be fluent and empty. She had learned this year that she could produce fluency the way other people produced small talk, and that it got A's and meant nothing, and that Mr. Bianchi, who read with a pencil and wrote things like "say the harder true thing," could tell the difference.

At lunch the next day she spread her notes between Ali's tray and Bryson's. "Here's my problem," she said. "If I ascribe the column to tradition, if I say she's borrowing Greek gravitas to dignify suffering, that's a critique. But it might be wrong. It might be more cerebral than that, or less. Maybe it's plainer than I want it to be."

"Plainer how," Bryson said, stealing one of her fries, which was his way of paying attention.

"Like, her spine actually broke. She was in an accident, she had surgeries, she wore corsets. The column might not be a metaphor at all. It might just be the truest way she could paint a spine that had cracked." Julia looked at the reproduction in her book, the fissure running through the landscape behind the figure, echoing the fissure in the body. "And the composition keeps doing this. The tear in the earth, the tear in her torso, the cracks in the column. Everything rhymes. So how do I say which is symbol and which is just structure?"

Ali turned the book toward herself. "You could say you don't know," she offered, careful, like handing someone a cup of water. "Not everything in a critique has to land."

Bryson shook his head. "Bianchi hates weasel words."

"There's a difference," Julia said slowly, "between weaseling and being accurate." She was thinking of her mother, who had been laid off in the spring and had spent the summer in a strange suspended brightness, applying for jobs, repotting plants, a whole interregnum between the life that ended and the one that hadn't started. Julia had wanted to call it hope and had wanted to call it fear, and it had refused both words. Some things were in between on purpose.

In the art room after school, Mr. Bianchi was rolling up the projector screen. She asked him whether a formal analysis could end in uncertainty. He didn't launch into anything; he just pulled a stool over with his foot and sat. "What's the uncertainty?"

"Whether the Ionic column is symbolic or literal. Whether she ascribed meaning to it, or whether it's just what a broken spine is, when you have to paint it."

"Which do you believe?"

"Both," Julia said. "That's the problem. My draft wants one, and the painting wants both, I think. The colour does it too. The flesh is pale and the ground is green and the column is this clean grey-white, like it belongs to a different world than the body does, but the nails are silver and they're everywhere, like the column is being held in, like the body's a frame around it." She heard herself accelerating and made herself stop. "I can describe that. I can't decide what it adds up to."

Mr. Bianchi was quiet long enough that she could hear the janitor's cart again, closer now. "Then write the description," he said, "and write the two readings, and write what stays open. If you close it falsely, I'll know, and worse, you'll know." He stood and unrolled the screen again, smoothing the print flat with the side of his hand. "Leave the tape alone, I just fixed it."

She stayed while he gathered his keys. At the door he paused, nodding at the print. "You looked at it for a long time today. Most students look for symbols. You looked at her."

On the bus home, Julia wrote at the top of a clean page: The spine is a cracked Ionic column, visible through an opening in the body. Under it she wrote: this is not only a symbol. Then she crossed out "only" and left the line sitting there, both readings still folded inside it, and watched the houses slide past, each one holding someone's in-between hour.

In the kitchen her mother was at the table with the laptop, applications open, and she looked up. "How was school?"

Julia set the printout of the painting beside the keyboard. "Do you see a building in her chest, or a spine?"

Her mother pulled her glasses down, leaned in, and touched the edge of the paper. "Both," she said. "Definitely both."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: White coat hypertension is when blood pressure reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home, so doctors may check it with home or all-day monitoring.
story:
The health lodge at Camp Wenatchee had one air conditioner, and it rattled like a swamp cooler with a grudge. Alexandra had volunteered for the junior aide program mostly because her mother wanted her to do something "medically adjacent" before she declared a major in the fall, and partly because the lodge had that air conditioner. On the second Wednesday, Mr. Sow, the camp's nurse, handed her a worn cuff and a stethoscope that smelled of pencil shavings.

"Sit," he said. "I'm the patient. Take my pressure."

She wrapped the cuff above his elbow, pressed the diaphragm to the crease of his arm, and squeezed the bulb until the needle climbed past one-sixty. Easing the valve, she listened for the first thump and the last one, the way the manual showed, and read the dial. "One twenty-four over seventy-eight." Mr. Sow nodded once and rolled down his sleeve. "Again on Friday," he said. "And by then you'll tell me what the numbers actually are. Not just say them. Explain them."

That night in the infirmary annex, Alexandra spread out the photocopies he had given her. Systolic, the top number, was the pressure when the heart pushed blood out; diastolic was the pressure between beats. She read it three times, then read the next page, about how salt held water in the vessels and how regular exercise lowered resting pressure over weeks and months, so that a person who walked daily might watch the top number drift down ten points by the end of a summer. She copied the words into her notebook without fully believing them, the way she copied formulas before she understood what they described.

The trouble started with Genesis. Genesis had signed up for the kayak program and needed a health clearance form stamped, which meant a pressure reading, and Genesis hated medical anything. She sat on the paper-covered cot twisting the drawstring of her shorts and told Alexandra about fainting during a vaccination in seventh grade, twice, in detail, while Alexandra found her pulse with two fingers.

"Stop talking about fainting," Alexandra said.

"I can't. If I stop thinking about it I'll think about it."

The cuff hissed, the needle swung, and Alexandra listened. The first knock came late, near one-forty on the dial. She took the reading again to be sure, because a number that high in a seventeen-year-old who had just swum two miles the day before seemed like an oxymoron, fitness and hypertension in the same body. It read the same both times. Genesis went pale in a way that had nothing to do with the number, and her breathing turned shallow and obstreperous, loud enough that two campers waiting outside the screen door looked in.

Mr. Sow came back from his rounds, took the slip of paper Alexandra handed him, and studied it. "You took this correctly?"

"Twice."

He looked at Genesis for a long moment, at the white knuckles, at the shorts drawstring wound into a spiral around her index finger. Then he set the paper down and asked, "Do you have readings from anywhere else? Home, a school physical, anything?"

Genesis unwound the string. "My mom has one of those cuffs on the kitchen counter. She uses it. I did it once in March because I was bored. It was, like, one-ten."

"Bring me a week of home readings," Mr. Sow said. "Morning and evening, write them down. If they're all like that, we'll talk. If they're only like this, in here, that's a different animal."

Alexandra followed him to the supply shelf afterward. "What's a different animal?"

He was counting gauze pads and didn't turn around. "Look it up in the binder. Page forty."

She looked it up. White coat hypertension, the page said: blood pressure that reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but reads normal at home, and because of that, doctors may check it with home readings or with monitoring across a whole day instead of trusting the single office number. Alexandra read it twice, then went to the window. Genesis was outside on the porch steps, holding the borrowed home cuff in a plastic bag Mr. Sow had given her, already rolling up her sleeve to try it in the open air where nobody wore a white coat or anything like one.

Alexandra thought about her own pages, the salt and the walking, the numbers drifting down over a season. Those were steady causes producing steady effects, patient work rewarded in small increments. This was something else, a number that told you more about the room than about the body in it. She had walked into the annex believing a reading was a fact about a heart, the way a thermometer reading was a fact about a fever. Now she had two frameworks and no clean way to weld them: bodies changed slowly through diet and exercise, and instruments changed sharply through fear, and a single number couldn't tell you which story it belonged to. She couldn't prognosticate from one reading, and she was beginning to suspect nobody honestly could.

That was the thing she said to Mr. Sow on Friday, when he sat down again and held out his arm. She took his pressure, one twenty-six over eighty, and then instead of reciting the pages she told him about the two stories, the slow one and the fast one, and admitted she didn't know yet how a person weighing them decided when a number meant a life and when it meant a Tuesday.

Mr. Sow rolled down his sleeve and stood up. "You'll figure out when to ask which question. That's most of the job." He pulled the screen door open and held it. "Go find out what Genesis wrote down."

Alexandra crossed the lawn to the porch, where Genesis sat with the notebook open on her knees, seven days of morning and evening numbers in careful columns, every one of them ordinary. Genesis held it up before Alexandra could ask. "It's the office," she said. "It was always the office." Alexandra sat down beside her and started at the top of the column, reading each number out loud.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Computing a binary search's midpoint as (low + high) / 2 can overflow on very large arrays; writing low + (high - low) / 2 gives the same middle without the overflow.
story:
Hassan's basement smelled like microwave popcorn and cold electronics, which was its own kind of comfort, the way certain basements reify the idea of "weekend" into something you could almost hold. Joshua set his laptop on the ping-pong table, next to a paddle someone had left as a monument to the last time anyone down here had done anything athletic. The regional programming competition was in eleven days, and their team had exactly one problem left to solve, the one with the sorted array of up to two billion entries and a clock that permitted no laziness.

"You still explaining it wrong," Kayley said, spinning in the office chair she had claimed by right of having brought the better snacks. "Watch. Say the dictionary. You want the word 'marmalade.' Linear search, you start at A and read every page until you get there. Binary search, you open the book in the middle, see 'kumquat,' and now you've thrown away half the dictionary in one move."

"I know how it works," Joshua said. "I have to explain it out loud to the judges, that's the part I'm bad at. The words. Not the logic."

"Same thing," Hassan said from the beanbag, where he was quality-testing the popcorn with the seriousness of a customs officer. "If you can't say it, you don't actually know it. Granddad says that. It's probably a colloquialism from wherever he's from, but it's true anyway."

Joshua pulled up their solution and walked through it, narrating like a nervous tour guide. Sorted data, he said, is what makes the halving legal; you compare against the middle element and you know which half to keep, so linear search's step-by-step trudge becomes a sequence of cuts, each one eliminating half of everything left over. Kayley made him say it twice more, once without saying "um" and once without touching the keyboard, and by the third run-through it came out almost smooth. He allowed himself the small pleasure of feeling competent, which in this basement was a rare and fragile currency.

Then Hassan sat up out of the beanbag like a man surfacing. "Wait, run the big one."

They had a test file from last year's competition, a monster dataset a previous team had downloaded and never deleted. Joshua's program ate the sample tests all afternoon, ten entries, a hundred, a thousand, each search snapping shut like a well-made trap. He pointed it at the two-billion-entry file. The progress bar crawled, the fan on the laptop rose to a small desperate whine, and then the program crashed with an error that looked, at first glance, like the machine itself had given up on the whole enterprise.

"No," Joshua said. "No, no, it worked. It worked on everything."

"It works until it doesn't," Hassan said, dragging his chair over. He scrolled the code with one hand, still holding popcorn in the other, which Joshua chose not to comment on because Hassan had a frightening talent for finding bugs. Hassan's finger stopped on one line, the midpoint calculation, the arithmetic that decided where the middle of the current range was. "There. That's where it died."

Joshua stared at the line. "That's just the middle. Low plus high, divided by two."

"On the giant array," Hassan said, "low plus high isn't just a number anymore. Add them together and you're asking for something enormous before you halve it. Try it the other way. Same middle, no addition of the two big numbers."

Kayley leaned in, and for a moment all three of them were quiet, which in this basement was practically a religious event. Joshua rewrote the line, subtracting first, taking half of the difference, adding that back to the low end. It felt almost like cheating, the way elegant things often do, as if the universe should have charged more for them. He ran the two-billion-entry file again. The fan complained, the bar crawled, and the search finished, correct, intact, alive.

"So explain it to me," Kayley said, spinning the chair to face him fully, "because the judges will ask. You found the bug. Tell me what you'd say."

Joshua thought about Mr. Menon, their computer science teacher, who had a habit of saying "correct is a floor, not a ceiling" and who would, if he ever saw their first version, probably frame it as a warning for future classes without ever naming them. Joshua had wanted, all week, to compress everything into something clean and finished, a neat story where the right answer arrives and stays arrived. But the honest version was messier: his program had worked, and then it hadn't, and the difference between the two had lived in one line of arithmetic he'd written without thinking. He tried it out loud. "The straightforward midpoint fails on huge arrays, because adding low and high together can overflow. You write it as low plus the difference, halved, and you get the same middle without that risk. I got it wrong first, and a teammate caught it, and I'd tell the judges exactly that, because pretending I saw it myself would be a lie with a shelf life of about one question."

"Endemic," Hassan said happily. "Overconfident midpoint code is endemic. Everybody writes it. You're not special."

"I'm a little special."

"You're a little special," Kayley agreed, in the tone people reserve for dogs who have finally learned to sit.

Joshua copied the fixed file three times, onto a flash drive, onto the cloud, onto Hassan's ancient desktop as a final redundancy, because distrust of any single machine was, after today, a philosophy he intended to keep. It was eleven at night when his phone buzzed, his mother asking if he planned to live in the basement now, and he typed back two more minutes and did not move. Kayley had opened the practice problem set again, and on the screen the next question was already loading, its sample input scrolling down in a long gray river.

"Same deal," she said, patting the chair beside her. "You debug, I time you, Hassan judges the popcorn-to-code ratio. Go."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: A binary search of one million sorted items needs at most 20 comparisons, because halving one million twenty times leaves a single item.
story:
Grandpa's dictionary sat on the stand by the armchair like a lectern, and Cohen had been staring at it for a week before he understood what it was teaching him. He was staying at the house while his father recuperated from surgery, and the afternoons had a slow shape to them: the clock ticking in the kitchen, the smell of old paper and coffee, the endless stretch of hours between lunch and dinner. Ms. Halvorsen, the retired teacher next door, had lent him a paperback on algorithms, and he had been reading a chapter about searching while the rain came down on the porch screens.

The problem was a bet. London had texted him a challenge on Tuesday: a million-entry word list, sorted alphabetically, one target word, two searchers. London would check the list in order from the beginning. Cohen could do whatever he wanted. Isla had volunteered to run the timer, since she claimed neither of them trusted the other. The race was set for Saturday, when London and Isla were coming out on the bus to visit. Cohen had the list on his laptop already, a grey column of words that scrolled longer than he could hold in his mind.

He told Grandpa about the bet while they ate sandwiches at the kitchen table. Grandpa pushed his glasses up and looked at the dictionary on its stand. "You ever watch me find a word in there?" he said. "I don't start at A." Cohen said he opened it somewhere in the middle too, everyone did, and Grandpa shrugged like that proved the whole argument and went back to his sandwich. It annoyed Cohen, the shrug, because he knew there was something underneath it and Grandpa wouldn't hand it over.

So he worked it out at the card table by the window, with the paperback open and a legal pad in front of him. If the list was sorted, then any word he looked at told him which half to throw away. The word either came before it or after it; the middle either was it or wasn't. One comparison cut a million entries to half a million. Another cut that half to a quarter. He wrote the numbers down the pad, dividing by two each time, and watched the column fall: five hundred thousand, two hundred fifty, one hundred twenty-five thousand, on and down until the row read one. He counted the rows. Twenty. Twenty comparisons and a million sorted items were down to a single one, found or not found. He sat back and heard the rain on the glass and thought about London, who was planning to start at entry one.

He practiced. He wrote the loop out by hand first, then typed it, and when it failed the first time because he'd mixed up which boundary moved, he fixed it and it failed again for a different reason, an off-by-one at the top edge, and he sat with the pad until the logic straightened itself out in his head. Isla called Thursday night to ask whether the whole thing was fair, since London was her friend too and she didn't want a putative victory that everyone would argue about afterward. Cohen said the rules were the rules: in order, from the top, one entry at a time. She said fine, and then asked if there would be food.

Saturday came in bright and cold. Grandpa made cocoa and put out the tin of shortbread he saved for occasions, and Ms. Halvorsen came over in her cardigan to watch, settling into the armchair with the dictionary at her elbow. Isla set her phone between the two laptops on the dining room table and read the rules aloud in a formal voice, like a referee. London cracked his knuckles. "Straight down the list," he said. "Old school. Someone's got to do the honest work." Cohen said nothing, because there was a small part of him, and he could admit this to himself, that wondered if twenty was actually right or just a number he'd talked himself into on the legal pad.

Isla said go. London's scroll blurred with speed, his finger on the trackpad, the counter on his screen climbing through the thousands. Cohen ran his code once. It printed a middle word, threw half the list away, printed another, and he watched the field narrow the way water drains from a sink, each step smaller and faster than the last. On the nineteenth comparison the code paused, checked, and the twentieth was the word. "Found it," Cohen said. Isla stopped the timer and looked at the two screens and then at London's counter, which read three hundred eleven thousand and something, still climbing.

"Twenty," London said, flat. "You found it in twenty." He scrolled back up and looked at Cohen's output, all the halved ranges printed in a column, and then at his own screen, and pushed his chair back from the table. Ms. Halvorsen leaned forward and touched the dictionary on its stand. "Faster than me, even," she said. Grandpa came in from the kitchen with the cocoa and set the tray down between the laptops. "Twenty," Cohen said again, mostly to himself, turning the legal pad around so London could see the column of numbers ending in one. London pulled his chair back in and held out his hand for the pad.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Thomas Carlyle's The French Revolution: A History, published in 1837, stressed the moral choices of individuals rather than impersonal historical forces.
story:
Olivier had promised Ms. O'Brien the draft by Monday, which meant Sunday had to be the day, and Sunday had already half evaporated into helping his father carry boxes down from the attic. The boxes belonged to his grandfather, who had died in the spring, and whose study was being emptied so the room could become something else, though nobody had said what. Inside the third box, under a stack of National Geographics held together with rotting rubber bands, Olivier found a fat brown book with the title stamped in faded gold: The French Revolution: A History, by Thomas Carlyle. He sat down on the hallway floor with it, forgetting the boxes entirely.

"Is that Grandpa's?" his mother asked, stepping over him with a lamp.

"I think so. It's Carlyle. Published in 1837, it says." He turned the stiff pages. "I'm literally writing about this."

"Then it's yours now," she said, and carried the lamp into the crepuscular end of the hall, where the afternoon light never quite reached and the wallpaper had darkened to the color of weak tea.

The essay was supposed to be historiographical, a word Olivier had underlined twice in Ms. O'Brien's assignment sheet: not what happened in the Revolution, but how what people said about it had changed since 1800. He had a pile of library printouts on his desk, Marxists and revisionists and counter-revisionists, each one correcting the last, and he had been trying for two days to make them march in a straight line. They refused. Now here was Carlyle, older than all of them, writing like a man narrating a thunderstorm. Olivier read a page about the fall of the Bastille and felt like he was reading scripture, or a very long dramatic monologue. There was almost no argument. There were people, strutting and suffering and choosing.

He called Sidney, who was writing the same essay and claimed to be three paragraphs from done.

"How do you organize yours?" Olivier asked. "Mine keeps turning into a list of people disagreeing with each other."

"That's what it is," Sidney said. "My brother says you just pick a lens and admit the others exist. Mine's about how the Marxist reading kind of underwrites everything after it, even the people who attack it. Like they're only attacking it because it's the building they're standing on."

Olivier looked at the Carlyle on his desk. "But what about before Marx? This Carlyle guy in 1837 doesn't care about forces at all. It's all moral choices. Danton decides something, Mirabeau decides something, and that's the history. It's like a play where the structure is just, people being people."

"Sounds unbearable," Sidney said. "Is it good?"

"It's completely insane and I couldn't stop reading it," Olivier said, which was true, and which was also the problem.

Connor came over that evening, ostensibly to study and actually to eat the leftover pad thai, and read two pages of Carlyle aloud in a theatrical whisper until Olivier confiscated the book. But when Olivier explained the essay, Connor tilted his chair back in the way that meant he was about to say something obvious.

"So your first section is Carlyle saying it's all individual moral choices, and then the twentieth century says no, it's impersonal forces, economics and all that, and then some people swing back partway. You don't have to pick. You just have to say what each one can see that the others can't."

"That's not a position, though."

"It's a position about positions," Connor said, and stole the last of the pad thai.

Olivier worked until midnight, then slept badly, then woke at six with the deadline pressing on him like weather. He wrote the Carlyle section first because it was the most alive in his head: a history from 1837 built out of individuals and their moral choices, dramatic to the point of embarrassment, and yet something in it kept its grip. Then he wrote forward, showing how later historians moved toward structures and systems, toward a utilitarianism of causes in which what mattered was not anyone's conscience but the aggregate conditions under which millions acted. He found he could hold both. What he could not do, even by eleven that morning, was decide whether Carlyle had been superseded or had simply been asking a different question, one that the structural historians had silenced rather than answered.

He handed in the draft with a final paragraph that said exactly that, then hated it, then decided it was more honest than a conclusion he did not believe. Ms. O'Brien read the first page while he stood there.

"Is this your grandfather's copy?" she asked, touching the brittle spine.

"It was. Why, does it matter?"

"It matters to you," she said, and kept reading.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: The legal age of consent differs by country and even between US states, and in many places it falls between 16 and 18.
story:
The bathroom mirror in the community center had a crack running through its lower left corner, and Mackenzie had decided to practice her talk to the crack rather than to her own face, because the crack would not look back at her with expectation. She set her phone on the sink edge, timer off, and began. "Consent is a yes you can take back," she said, "and it has to be a yes you're free to give." Her voice came out flatter than she wanted. She tried again, louder, and a woman drying her hands at the second sink gave her a look and left.

She had agreed to run this session three weeks ago, after a night she still turned over like a stone in her pocket. The nurse at the clinic had been younger than Mackenzie expected, brisk and sagacious in a way that made questions feel pre-answered, and Mackenzie had gone in for nothing, really, just a check that she was fine, and come out with pamphlets and the thought that nobody had ever told her any of it plainly. Not the nurse's fault. Nobody had told anybody. So when the youth coordinator asked for peer volunteers, Mackenzie heard herself say yes before she had finished deciding.

A knock rattled the door. "Kenzie, it's us," Hayden said. "You've been in there forever."

She let them in, locking the door behind them, and Hayden immediately began to exhume materials from the cavern of a backpack: creased pamphlets, a shoebox of demonstration kits, a flip pad from a workshop two years ago. "You don't need all of it," Mederick said, leaning against the stall. "You'll talk for nine hours and they'll just want the free condoms."

"I want it right," Mackenzie said. She spread the pamphlets across the sink counter. Contraception, she explained, because Hayden kept saying the pill as though it were the whole subject, one method standing in for all of them, a synecdoche that she knew would leak into her talk if she wasn't careful. She tapped each one. Hormonal methods, barrier methods, the implant, the IUD, where you got each and what a failure actually looked like. Then testing. "Chlamydia and gonorrhea, a urine sample," she said. "HIV and syphilis, blood. Most of it's painless. Most of it's curable, and the rest is treatable."

"You've memorized the pamphlet," Hayden said, half admiring.

"I went. Last month. That's how I know." She hadn't planned to say that. The bathroom was quiet except for the drip of the tap, and she watched the two of them recalibrate her in their heads, and let them.

It was Mederick who found the flashcard. He'd been fanning them out on the radiator like a card trick, and he stopped at one. "This says age of consent, eighteen. That's not right."

"It's right here."

"It's not right everywhere." He sat up on the radiator, heels against the pipe. "I was at my grandpa's over spring break, in Ireland, and there was a thing in the paper about a court case, and I asked him and he looked it up. It's seventeen there. I nearly fell over. Same as us being eighteen, except a whole year different."

Mackenzie took the card back and turned it over, as though the other side might have a footnote waiting. "So it changes."

"Between countries," Mederick said. "And I asked him about the States, because my cousin moved to Connecticut, and he said it's not even the same from one state to another. Different states, different ages." He shrugged. "Some places it's sixteen. He said in a lot of places it lands somewhere between sixteen and eighteen."

Mackenzie stood very still with the card in her hand, thinking about how she had written eighteen in her own handwriting, in what she'd believed was a fact and not a local fact, a rule that fit her the way her street address fit her. She thought of the talk she'd given the mirror an hour ago, confident, cracked but confident. "Okay," she said slowly, "so the card is wrong, or the card is right only here, and I can't tell which of those it is from inside this bathroom."

"You'd better decide," Hayden said, glancing at the clock above the door. "You're on in ten minutes."

She took out her phone and searched, holding the screen low so the cracked mirror wouldn't reflect it back at her. Mederick was right. Different countries, different ages; different even between the states; in many places it fell between sixteen and eighteen, and only in some, like hers, at the line she'd been standing behind all her life. She read it twice, then a third time, not because she doubted the screen but because she wanted to feel the shape of the doubt itself, the difference between a rule you've been handed and a rule you've checked.

"Here's what I'll say," she said, gathering the pamphlets into a stack and squaring them against the counter. "The number depends on where you are, and that's not a loophole, that's a reason to know where you are. And the legal part isn't the whole of it anyway, because you can be over any line they draw and still not want something, and the law doesn't fix that. Consent is the yes. The number is just where the law starts counting." She paused, hearing herself, hearing all the places she was still unsure. "That part I'm still working on. Maybe I'll tell them that too."

Hayden held the door. "You'll be great," they said, which was not the same as you're right, and Mackenzie knew the difference, and went out anyway, stack under her arm.

Mederick caught her in the hallway and pressed the flashcard into her palm, the wrong one, the one that said eighteen plain as a street sign. "Keep it," he said. "So you remember to check."

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: François Furet's 1978 book, translated as Interpreting the French Revolution, argued the French should stop treating the Revolution as the key to all of modern French history.
story:
The library closed at nine, and Mr. Russo had already warned her twice that he meant it this time. Elizabeth spread her photocopies across the table by the window, where the late light came through in long orange bars, and tried to decide whether her essay on the French Revolution had an argument or only a pile of quotations. It was due at eight the next morning. She had eleven hours, and two of those belonged to sleep if she was honest with herself.

"You look like you're building a bomb," Jocelyn said, dropping into the chair across from her with a slushie that was already sweating rings onto the wood.

"Kind of." Elizabeth slid a page toward her. "It's about how historians changed their minds. Everybody used to agree about what the Revolution meant, and then they stopped, and nobody's really agreed since."

Delphine arrived a minute later with her own stack of books, because Delphine was taking the same class and had chosen, characteristically, to do the identical assignment at the identical table rather than somewhere quieter. She read over Elizabeth's shoulder without asking. "You've got Soboul here eulogizing the sans-culottes like they were saints, and then this other guy saying the whole thing was theater. Those don't go together."

"That's the point. That's what I'm trying to write about." Elizabeth heard how thin it sounded. The problem was that she had a topic but not a position, and Mr. Russo had circled her last thesis in red and written, in the margin, So what do you think, and why?

She turned back to the fattest photocopy, the one she'd made from a chapter of a book translated from the French, written by a historian named François Furet. Her grandfather had a battered copy of it on his shelf, and last Sunday, sitting in his kitchen while the radio muttered, she had tried to explain to him what she was working on. He'd poured her coffee she didn't drink and asked very good questions, the kind that reveal how little you know.

"So in 1978," she had told him, turning the book so its cover faced him, "Furet published this. Interpreting the French Revolution, in English. And his argument was that the French should stop treating the Revolution as the key to all of modern French history. Like, everything after 1789 was supposed to be explained by it. He said that was the problem."

Her grandfather had tapped the cover. "And did they? Stop?"

"I don't know yet. I think some did." She had felt the gap open under her, the ordinary feeling of almost understanding something.

Now, under the window with the light going gray, she read the pages again. Jocelyn had drifted off to the fiction shelves; Delphine was highlighting with the concentration of a virtuoso, her marker moving in long unbroken strokes, never once crossing a line she hadn't meant to cross. Elizabeth watched her for a moment, oddly calmed by it, and then wrote at the top of a fresh page: What if the disagreement itself is the subject?

She worked without talking for forty minutes. The clock above the reference desk said 7:21 when she sat back. What she had written was this: the Marxist historians had one story, Furet had another, and she, Elizabeth, seventeen, owed neither of them loyalty. She thought Furet was right that a single event shouldn't have to carry all of modern history on its back, like one igneous rock asked to explain the whole mountain. But she also thought the older historians were right that the Revolution's violence and its hopes were real, and that a person could hold both of those views at once, or at least hold them close enough together to feel their heat.

"Read it to me," Delphine said, capping her marker.

Elizabeth read the last paragraph aloud, quietly, because a man two tables over was asleep against a newspaper. When she finished, Delphine said, "You say 'I think' four times in two sentences."

"That's on purpose. I don't want to pretend I'm sure."

Mr. Russo came by at ten to nine with his keys already out, jingling them like a warning. "Packing up, scholars." Outside, the streetlights had come on, and the air smelled like rain on hot pavement. Jocelyn had left her slushie cup, which had melted into a red puddle shaped vaguely like France.

Elizabeth stacked her pages, and the top one slid off and landed face-up on the table. She picked it up, looked at the sentence she'd underlined twice, and put it in her bag with the rest.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Cheating out means an actor turns their body partly toward the audience, even while talking to another character, so their face and voice carry.
story:
Payton had cleared the garage on Saturday morning before anyone else was awake, dragging the lawnmower against the wall and taping a rectangle of masking tape on the concrete floor to stand in for the stage. By ten, seven folding chairs faced the rectangle, which was meant to be the audience. By ten-thirty, only Andreanne had arrived, holding a printed script with the pages already soft at the corners.

"You know nobody's going to show," Andreanne said, sitting in one of the chairs and putting her feet on another. "It's Saturday. Devon's at his cousin's. The twins are at the twins' thing."

"They said they'd come." Payton checked her phone. There was a message from Alishba, sent at 9:52: "omw. also i invited Mr. Morningstar bc you need an adult witness when everything inevitably collapses. jk. mostly." Payton read it twice and did not know whether to laugh or hide the tape rectangle under a tarp.

Alishba arrived with a bag of clementines and, behind her, Mr. Morningstar from next door, still in his gardening shirt, holding a thermos like a man who had been promised entertainment. He sat at the back, which Payton understood immediately was a power move, because the back was where a director could not see him without turning all the way around.

They ran the first scene anyway, with Andreanne playing every missing part, spinning between positions like a weather vane. It was, Payton admitted to herself, profligate with energy, all that sprinting for three lines of dialogue, and funny enough that Mr. Morningstar laughed into his thermos twice. But when Andreanne delivered the lead's big speech facing the empty chair that stood for the other character, Payton, watching from the chairs, could see only the back of her head. The words arrived fine. The face did not exist.

"Turn," Payton said. "No, toward me. Halfway."

Andreanne turned her whole body toward the chairs and abandoned the other character entirely. "Like this? Now I'm talking to the wall."

"Not the wall. The audience. But keep talking to her." Payton got up and stood where the empty chair was, then walked the diagonal herself, feeling the geometry of it. "Sort of angled. Both at once."

Alishba peeled a clementine from the third chair. "My brother calls that cheating out. Cheating out means you turn your body partly toward the audience even while you're talking to another character, so your face and voice carry." She said it with the flat certainty of someone quoting an older sibling and hoping to be corrected.

"Then cheat out," Payton said. She wrote it in the margin of her script, CO, in small letters, next to every line that had been swallowed by the back of a head. When Andreanne ran the speech again, half-turned, something odd happened: the confession in the speech suddenly seemed performed, offered, given away rather than blurted. Payton sat very still in her chair. She had asked for a technical fix and gotten an interpretation, as if the actor's body had an opinion about who the speech was really for.

Here was the problem she had not anticipated. Her English teacher had drilled into her that the play was private, interior, two people locked in a room at the end of something. Cheating out made the room leak. It handed the moment to strangers in chairs. Payton walked the rectangle twice with her hands in her hoodie pocket, and Andreanne, dripping sweat in November, said, "Payton. Verdict. I have a life."

"Both," Payton said finally. "Cheat out on the lines that ask for something. Stay closed on the ones that hide." She was not sure this was a real directing principle or something she had just invented, and she said so out loud, because pretending certainty had always seemed to her a way to aggrandize a guess into a rule. "It might be wrong. We'll look at it in the chairs."

"That's not an answer," Andreanne said, but she ran it both ways, and even Mr. Morningstar leaned forward, which from the back row was practically a standing ovation.

The second problem was smaller and more concrete: the twins arrived at noon with the news that Devon was not coming, that Devon claimed he had a disincentive, namely that Payton had once told him his reading of the second monologue was "a choice." Payton composed a message while the others ate clementines on the tape rectangle, their sneakers on the corners of the stage like trespassers. "Devon. I said it was a choice because it was a good one and I was jealous of it. Also you have the best voice in the cast and if I have to replace you I will play the part myself and everyone will suffer. Come tomorrow at four. Bring the monologue. I'll bring my apology face." She read it over, deleted "apology face," put it back, and sent it.

Mr. Morningstar refilled his thermos from a watering can of coffee that appeared to have no bottom and told them about a one-act he had acted in during high school, in which a boy playing a butler exited through a wall instead of the door and the whole production was revised around the wall. "We called it the fourth wall for weeks afterward," he said. "As though we had discovered it."

At four the next day, in the same garage, the full cast stood inside the rectangle, and Devon, who had come, stood half-turned toward the folding chairs, face open, voice carrying all the way to the lawnmower. Payton sat in the front row with her marked-up script and said, "Again. From where she enters. And this time, when you tell her, don't give it to us. Keep it for her."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: Murmansk, a Russian port north of the Arctic Circle, stays ice-free all year because of warm water carried by the North Atlantic Current.
story:
The map covered most of the back wall of Ms. Brown's classroom, its currents drawn as fat ribbons of red and blue, and Ethan had been assigned to explain one of them on Friday. The red ribbon was the Gulf Stream, the label said, curling off Florida toward the gray rectangle of Europe. He had read the textbook chapter twice and still felt like he was reciting a stranger's phone number.

He stayed after the bell on Wednesday, partly for the map and partly because Dominik was there, and Dominik actually understood these things. Dominik was tracing the eastern edge of the Atlantic with one finger, north of Scandinavia, into a region of small white ports printed close together along a Russian coast.

"Why are there so many ports up there?" Dominik asked. "That's basically the top of the world. Doesn't it freeze?"

"Everything freezes up there," Ethan said. "Look at the latitude line. That's inside the Arctic Circle."

Dominik tapped a name on the coast. "Murmansk. So this is locked in ice all winter, right?"

Ethan leaned in to see. He had his notebook open, the chapter summary half copied, and something about the shape of the red ribbon was bothering him. It didn't stop at Europe. It bent northeast, splitting into branches, one of which ran up along Norway and kept going. He followed it with his finger and it aimed, more or less, at the exact coast Dominik was touching.

"Hold on," Ethan said.

"What?"

"The current goes up there. That's the whole thing I'm supposed to explain, that warm water crossing the Atlantic. But the map's saying it doesn't just warm Britain, it goes way past." He checked the chapter's inset map, the one with temperature shading. The warm tongue of color stretched farther north than anywhere else at that latitude. Murmansk, a Russian port north of the Arctic Circle, stayed ice-free all year because of warm water carried by the North Atlantic Current. That was the caption, in small print, and Ethan read it twice because it seemed absurd. He said it out loud so Dominik could hear it, pointing at the port and then at the ribbon connecting it to the tropics.

Dominik frowned at the wall. "So ships can reach Murmansk in January. In the Arctic. Because of water that started near Florida."

"That's what it says."

"That's either the coolest thing I've ever learned or a typo."

Ms. Brown was erasing the board, but she had gone quiet, and Ethan could feel her listening without turning around, the way she did when she wanted students to think they had discovered something on their own.

The problem was that his presentation, as drafted, stopped at the obvious. The Gulf Stream carries warm water north, therefore Western Europe is milder than Canada at the same latitude, therefore Britain has rain instead of tundra. All true, all flat. The Murmansk detail had done something to the shape of the idea in his head. He had been thinking of the current as an answer, a single fact that explained a single effect, the way you'd explain a heater warming one room. But the warm water didn't stop where the story usually stopped. It kept moving, branching, giving its heat away gradually across a whole ocean margin, and the effects fell where they fell, whether or not they fit a tidy national narrative. Britain wasn't specially chosen. Murmansk wasn't an anomaly. They were two points along one long release.

Yet he couldn't claim more than he could defend. The map showed the current reaching that coast, and the caption stated the connection, but the mechanisms underneath, why the water moved as it did, how much warmth arrived and how much mattered, were layers he hadn't touched. He'd read enough to know that some scientists argued the wind patterns mattered more than the water for Europe's winters, that the picture was contested in ways the textbook's confident ribbons concealed. The red line on the wall was a simplification of a simplification. He would say what the map showed, say where his confidence ended, and let the line between them be visible.

On Friday he stood up with the map projected behind him and told the class about the ribbon leaving Florida, and then, because Aurelia in the second row was shivering dramatically in her cardigan and complaining that the classroom was freezing, he started there. "You're cold right now because of air coming down from the north," he said. "Now watch what water does." He walked them across the Atlantic, Britain, Norway, and then the part he liked best. "Here's Murmansk, a Russian port north of the Arctic Circle. It stays ice-free all year because of warm water carried by the North Atlantic Current. In January, ships dock there."

"Ships," Aurelia said. "In the Arctic."

"That far north, everything else on that coast is locked in ice."

Dominik, from the back, raised his hand not to ask a question but to add, "It's either the coolest thing I've ever learned or a typo," and the class laughed, and Ethan laughed too.

"What I can't tell you," he said, when it quieted, "is exactly how much of Europe's mildness to credit to this current and how much to winds. People argue about it. The map makes it look settled. It isn't." He looked at the projected ribbon, running red and confident across the dark blue, and then at Aurelia, who was still rubbing her arms. "But somewhere near the top of the world there's a harbor with open water in January, and this line is why. Turn the projector off and look at the wall."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: ISO 216 paper sizes such as A4 have sides in the ratio of 1 to the square root of 2, so cutting a sheet in half gives two sheets of the same shape.
story:
Ryan had the whole table by the window, which was the only good thing about a Saturday spent at the public library. Spread across it were his sketches for the astronomy club's recruitment poster, a broken compass he refused to throw away because it had belonged to his grandfather, and two sheets of paper he had printed at fifteen cents a page: one A4, one A3. He had chosen the bigger size on purpose, thinking it would make his design of Orion look heroic instead of cramped. Instead the constellation had come out fat, its stars swollen like burns.

"You're staring at them like they insulted your mother," said Peyton, sliding into the chair across from him with a stack of returns. Peyton volunteered on Saturdays and considered the library, in her own phrase, an alluvial deposit of other people's interests, layer upon layer of what the town had wanted to read over fifty years. She set down her books. "What's wrong with your sky?"

"Everything's the wrong size. I drew it for the small one and then just told the printer to make it big, and now the belt of Orion looks like it ate the small Orion." Ryan held the A4 sheet over the A3, aligning corners. The stars didn't line up where he expected. They lined up somewhere else. He tilted his head, then flipped the small sheet sideways, and suddenly it sat against the big one edge to edge, the same shape exactly, as if the two sheets belonged to the same phylum and he had finally classified them correctly.

Peyton leaned in, chin on her fist. "Wait. Do that again."

He did it again. It worked again. It shouldn't have; he knew enough geometry to know that doubling a page should change its shape, the way a television screen and a movie screen are cousins, not siblings. But these were siblings. He pulled out his phone and measured the sheets against the screen edge, and the numbers came back the same ratio for both. He said the words aloud, slowly, like testing ice: "The sides are one to the square root of two."

"Which means?"

"Which means when you cut it in half, you get two sheets the same shape as the one you started with. That's the whole point of it. Somebody designed it that way." He felt the small, unreasonable delight of a rule discovered rather than told. Somewhere in a standards committee, decades before he was born, someone had thought about a person exactly like him, scaling a poster badly.

Mr. Greco, at the next table with his newspapers, cleared his throat without looking up. "In my day we called that a pleasant surprise, not a standard."

"It is a standard, though," Ryan said. "It's ISO 216. It's on the printer settings." He showed him the dropdown menu on the screen at the print station, A3, A4, A5 marching downward like a family.

Mr. Greco waved at his own eyes. "I take it on faith."

The problem was not the paper anymore. The problem was Ryan's original drawing, done freehand, done fast, done the night his father had asked whether the club was really worth the time now that college applications were tightening like a cuff. He had said yes without hesitating, and he had meant it, and he had also known that he was choosing a smaller version of a life he used to want at full scale. He looked at the two sheets, the small Orion and the big one, and thought about how his design had betrayed him precisely because he had not understood what he was scaling. Things did not just get bigger or smaller. They got bigger or smaller and kept their proportions, or they didn't, and you found out afterward.

"So fix the drawing," Peyton said, reading his face the way she shelved books, by section. "Redraw it at the small size, print it at the big one, done. It'll match perfectly. You just said so."

"It'll match," Ryan agreed. He picked up the broken compass, set its point, and began marking out the star positions again on a fresh A4 sheet, this time working from the corner rather than the center, because if the ratio was fixed he had to build the design inside its logic, not impose his own. Peyton watched him work for a while, then went to reshelve returns in the 500s, the science section, which she said was where astronomy went to be enfranchised among its fellow subjects after years of being treated as a hobby.

He was halfway through the redraw when he found it: the twist was that his original hadn't been wrong at all. The stars hadn't been fat because the printer ruined them. They were fat because he had drawn them fat, at midnight, exhausted, and the small size had hidden it. Enlargement had merely told the truth. He sat back and laughed, quietly, because the library was quiet and because it was funny in the specific way that only a person who has spent two hours blaming a machine can find funny.

Peyton came back with a cart and paused. "What?"

"Nothing. The printer was innocent."

"The printer is always innocent," she said. "It's the most innocent thing in this building." She pointed at his fresh sheet, where the belt of Orion sat slim and correct. "That one's better, though."

He fed the page into the machine, pressed the button for A3, and waited while the light slid beneath the glass. The sheet came out warm, and the hunter came out right, every star exactly where he had put him, only larger, only louder. He held the two versions side by side and thought about telling his father that the club had a hundred members now, which it did not, or that this poster would change that, which he could not promise. He rolled the big sheet into a tube instead, tucked the small one into his notebook as a record of the mistake, and left the broken compass on the table for whoever came next.

"Hey," Peyton called after him, "your grandpa's compass."

"Keep it," Ryan said. "It measures circles. I only need ratios now."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the second derivative test, if f'(a) = 0 and f''(a) is negative, the function has a local maximum at x = a.
story:
The problem was taped to the whiteboard before the bell finished ringing: a rectangle of farmland, three hundred meters of fence, one side open to the river. Mr. Holloway wanted the largest possible enclosure, and he wanted it by Friday. Paige copied the function into her notebook, h(x) = x(150 - x/2), and underlined it twice, because underlining felt like progress even when nothing else did.

She had expected calculus to be like algebra, a machine that ran the same way every time. Instead it kept asking her to decide things. Differentiating had gone all right; she had a clean little derivative, 150 - x, and she could see that it equaled zero when x was 150. But a number where the slope went flat could be a peak or a trough, and the worksheet offered no clue which. Hashim, two seats over, had already flipped his page and was sketching something with the smug economy of a boy who had done this before.

"How do you know it's the top of the hill?" she asked him. "It could be the bottom of a valley. The slope is zero both places."

Hashim shrugged. "You just graph it and look."

That answer sat badly with her. Graphing felt like cheating, a way of peeking at the answer instead of proving it, and she distrusted her own shaky sketches besides. Nikita leaned across the aisle with a different suggestion entirely, delivered in the low voice she reserved for opinions that could get them both detention.

"Ask Holloway," Nikita whispered. "That's what he's paid for."

"Then he explains it and I still don't own it," Paige said, and immediately wondered when she had become someone who talked about owning mathematics. Her mother would have called that reactionary, the way Paige rejected any method that hadn't come from her own head. But it wasn't quite that. She wasn't refusing help; she was refusing shortcuts.

That night she wrote an email to Nikita, because Nikita answered written things more honestly than spoken ones. "I don't want the answer," Paige typed. "I want to know how you'd decide whether the flat point is a maximum or a minimum without a graph. If you know, don't tell me the conclusion. Just tell me where to look." She sat with her finger over the send button, briefly tempted to introspect instead of acting, to spend the evening examining why she needed to do this alone rather than doing it. She sent the email, then opened her notebook anyway.

The reply came at ten forty. "Differentiate again," Nikita wrote. "The second derivative tells you which way the curve is bending at that point. It's called the second derivative test. The rest you can figure out. You always do." Paige read it three times. The second derivative. Of course. If the first derivative was the slope, the second was how the slope itself was changing, and a slope that was decreasing through zero meant the curve had stopped climbing and begun to fall. She almost wrote back to argue that this was more than a hint, then changed her mind mid-sentence. It was exactly a hint. It named a door without saying what was behind it.

She worked the algebra twice, because her arithmetic had been recalcitrant all week, dropping signs the way a nervous person drops keys. The second derivative came out to negative one half, small and unglamorous, and she stared at it for a long moment. Negative. At the critical point, where the first derivative was zero, the second was negative, and that meant the curve bent downward there, which meant the flat spot was a peak. A local maximum at x = 150. She checked the original function, multiplying it out, and there it was: the enclosure was widest exactly there, eleven thousand two hundred fifty square meters, and no other fence arrangement would beat it. She had not drawn a single graph.

Friday, Mr. Holloway called her to the board. She wrote the function, the first derivative, the zero, then paused with the chalk hovering. Part of her wanted to retreat to Hashim's method, to sketch the parabola and point, because the picture was safe and everyone understood pictures. Instead she wrote the second derivative, drew a circle around the negative sign, and said, "The second derivative test. It's negative where the first is zero, so it's a maximum." Mr. Holloway nodded once, without praise, which from him was the same thing.

Walking out, though, she felt the cost of it. Hashim fell into step beside her and she understood that she had solved the problem in a way he hadn't, and that this distance, small as it was, had opened between them like the fence between two fields. Nikita was already halfway down the corridor, not waiting, as if to prove she had never doubted the outcome. Paige fingered the email still saved on her phone, thinking she might delete it, or might keep it, and had not decided when Nikita turned around at the stairwell door.

"You going to the river this weekend?" Nikita called. "Bring your fence problem. I want to see you actually measure something for once."

"I'll bring the chalk," Paige said.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: Each feature in a GIS layer links to a row in an attribute table, so data such as the number of residents in each building can be totaled for a selected area.
story:
The departure board had been saying DELAYED next to Flight 1142 for two hours, and Lucas had metabolized the news in stages: first irritation, then boredom, and finally something like reluctant permission. His geography class was bound for a conference in Spokane where they were supposed to present their flood-risk project, and now the whole group was marooned at Gate C9 with vending machine crackers and time.

Mr. Yamamoto, who taught the GIS elective and had agreed to chaperone six students across three states, sat down beside Lucas with two coffees and handed one over. "The presentation doesn't wait for the plane," he said. "We present Thursday whether we're rested or not. Want to run it here?"

Lucas opened his laptop on the narrow seat between them. On the screen sat the map he had spent five weeks building: the city of Rockford rendered in pale parcels, the floodplain drawn over it in translucent blue, and beneath that a third layer, housing, each building a small polygon tagged with data. Miley leaned over the seatback from the row behind, and Hunter, who had been pacing the concourse like an obstreperous toddler denied a nap, dropped into the seat across the aisle.

"Go from the top," Miley said. "Pretend we're the town council."

Lucas began the way he always began, pointing at the overlap of blue and parcels. "So the flood zone intersects about four hundred structures," he said. "Which sounds bad, but the council will want to know what it actually means."

Hunter frowned at the screen. "It means four hundred houses get wet."

"Does it?" Miley asked. "Some of those polygons are apartment buildings. Some are garages."

That was the problem Lucas had been circling for a week without landing on. He had a count of buildings and no count of people, and the role-play scenario Mr. Yamamoto had written was specific: the mock council had a limited relocation budget and would vote on which neighborhoods to prioritize. A council member would ask him, to his face, how many residents lived in the flood zone. Not houses. Residents.

He clicked on one apartment building near the river, the old brick one on Elm Street, and a table opened beside the map. One row. Address, year built, units, residents. He clicked a second building and a second row appeared. He sat back, coffee cooling in his hand, staring at the two rows.

"Each feature in the layer links to a row in an attribute table," he said slowly, mostly to himself, and then, faster, as the shape of it assembled: "So if I select all the features inside the flood zone, I can total the residents column. It's already there. I just never asked for it."

Miley was already reaching for his keyboard. "Select by location. Do it."

He drew the selection, and every polygon inside the blue overlay lit up yellow, a sudden rash of highlighted buildings along the river and through the low eastern flats. The table repopulated itself with row after row, and at the bottom, when he asked for the sum of the residents field, the number came up: 6,214 people. Not four hundred wet houses. Six thousand two hundred and fourteen neighbors, most of them, when he sorted the data, living in the two cheapest neighborhoods in town.

Nobody said anything for a moment. Down the concourse a toddler was screaming about a pretzel, and a gate agent announced that Flight 1142 was now delayed a further hour.

Mr. Yamamoto sipped his coffee and said nothing, which Lucas had learned was his way of saying everything.

Hunter broke the silence. "So when the council asks how many houses are at risk, you tell them that's the wrong question."

"I want to be careful," Lucas said. "The number's only as good as the census data behind it, and I don't know how current it is. Some of those buildings might be empty. I can't verify every row." He paused. "But it's honest to say approximately six thousand people, and to say the uncertainty, than to say four hundred buildings and let them decide a budget on that."

While the others argued about slide order, Lucas pulled out his phone and typed a message to his mother, who was tracking his flight from home.

Stranded in Denver, presentation moved up, actually good news. Figured out the thing I was stuck on. Six thousand people live in the flood zone and I can prove it, or at least prove how I counted. Will explain when I land. Love you.

She replied within a minute, as she always did: Six thousand! That's more people than your whole school. Also your enthalpy homework is due Monday, don't forget it exists.

He laughed, and Miley asked what, and he turned the phone toward her. "She thinks chemistry still matters to me," he said. "The enthalpy worksheet. Due the day after we get back." He looked at his laptop, where the yellow buildings still glowed against the blue, and decided the worksheet would get done on the plane, or it wouldn't.

When the agent finally called Group 1, Lucas closed the laptop without shutting the map down. He wanted the number still waiting on the screen when he opened it again, in case he needed to check that it was real. He slung his bag over his shoulder and followed Miley toward the jet bridge, and behind him Hunter called out, "Six thousand, Lucas. Lead with the six thousand."

"Boarding," the agent said, and scanned his ticket.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) held that a public official suing for libel must prove actual malice: that the statement was known to be false or made with reckless disregard for truth.
story:
By the time I took my seat in the folding chairs at the back of the town hall, I had the case basically memorized. That's what I told Tyrone, anyway, on the steps outside, while he peeled the label off a bottle of water and said, "Sure you do." Ms. Papadopoulos had assigned me both sides of New York Times v. Sullivan for the mock court on Thursday, petitioner and respondent, eight minutes each, and I'd read the entire opinion twice, or most of it, or the good parts. The parts that mattered.

The meeting had drawn maybe sixty people, which for this town is a stadium crowd. On the agenda between the sewer bond and the pickleball court lighting was a Mr. Okafor, a county official, who wanted three minutes to discuss "a matter of defamation." He stood at the podium in a suit that fit like it had been bought for a thinner year and held up a copy of the Ledger, our newspaper, folded to page four.

"Two weeks ago this paper stated that I missed the budget vote," he said. "I did not miss it. I was in the hospital. They have printed a correction the size of a postage stamp, and I am telling you tonight that this cannot stand. This is an attempt to denigrate my character, and if it takes a lawsuit, then a lawsuit is what it will take."

The room did the thing rooms do, a low shifting murmur, and the moderator asked whether there was discussion. Tyrone leaned over and whispered, "There's your respondent brief, man. Write that down." I told him I'd already thought of it, which wasn't true in the way I said it, but it was true in spirit.

A woman near the front, who introduced herself as the paper's editor, stood up. She said the reporter had relied on a source at the county office, that the error was corrected within a day of learning otherwise, and that the paper regretted it. She said it in the flat, exhausted voice of someone who has apologized to a room before. Mr. Okafor said regret was not a defense, and he was right about that much, and he knew it, and you could see him knowing it, standing a little taller at the podium.

Here is where I got to be smarter than the room, which is a thing I enjoy more than I should probably admit. I raised my hand. The moderator called on me, and I stood up among the folding chairs like I was rising at the Supreme Court itself. "In New York Times v. Sullivan, in 1964, the Court held that when a public official sues for libel, he has to prove actual malice. That means the statement was known to be false when it was published, or made with reckless disregard for the truth."

The editor turned around in her seat to look at me. Mr. Okafor asked who I was. "Grayson. I'm arguing the case at the high school on Thursday." Somebody in the third row laughed, kindly or not, and the moderator said, "Thank you, young man," in the voice you use for a dog that has fetched something.

Walking out, Tyrone punched my arm. "You said 1964." "It was 1964." "Last week you told me it was 1966 and that Sullivan was the mayor of Montgomery." "I never said that." I had said that. I had said it with total confidence, in his driveway, holding a can of soda, and I had also told him the case stood for the proposition that newspapers could print whatever they wanted, which even I, on the walk home, understood was a revisionist account of a decision that had done something narrower and stranger. The Court hadn't let papers lie. It had made public officials carry a heavier burden than the rest of us, on the theory that the rest of us need to hear the arguing.

Cara was waiting by the door with her own brief folded under her arm, because Ms. Papadopoulos had assigned her the same case, opposite mine on the panel, which meant Thursday was going to be the two of us in front of judges from the county courthouse. She'd been in the back of the hall the whole time. "Nice cite," she said. "Now tell me the other side."

"Other side of what?"

"You just handed Okafor's opponent his whole argument. You're telling me a public official has to prove the paper knew it was false. Fine. But you're arguing Thursday that the paper should win. So what do you say when the judges ask you whether a paper can just make things up about elected officials and hide behind a standard nobody can ever meet?"

I said something about the marketplace of ideas, which is the kind of phrase that sounds like an answer and is really a way of buying time, and Cara waited, and I stopped talking, and we stood under the town hall's one working floodlight while the pickleball people filed past us to their agenda item.

"Here's what I've got," she said. "The reporter asked the county office and printed what they told her. She didn't know it was false. And it's hard to call that reckless when she asked the one place that would actually know." She shrugged. "Whether that's enough, I don't know. That's the part I can't figure out, honestly. What is reckless? Who counts?"

"That's the part I can't figure out either," I said, which was, for once, an accurate statement of my condition, and saying it out loud felt like setting down something I'd been carrying in one hand for a week.

The moderator's voice came through the propped door behind us, calling the vote on the sewer bond. Cara tucked her brief under her arm tighter and started toward the parking lot. "Thursday," she said. "Bring the 1964 version."

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
