fact: In 1966, Pope Paul VI's Paenitemini allowed national bishops' conferences to replace the traditional Catholic fast and abstinence with other penance, such as prayer and works of charity.
story:
Dominic set his phone on the kitchen counter, screen up, a scanned page of a Church document open on it, and went back to slicing onions for his grandmother. The debate was in four days. Theodore had drawn the affirmative: that the rule against meat on Fridays still binds Catholics today. Dominic had drawn the negative, and he had nothing except a vague memory of his friend Paul eating a hamburger on a Friday and not seeming afraid of hell.

"You're grinding that knife like it owes you recompense," his grandmother said from the doorway. She took the stool by the counter and began snapping the ends off green beans into a bowl.

"Sorry. I'm stuck." He laid the knife down. "Why do we still skip meat on Fridays? Paul's family doesn't, and they go to the same church we do."

She kept snapping beans. "Because your grandfather liked it that way, and after he died I kept on liking it. It's not complicated."

"It kind of is, though." He turned the phone toward her. "I found this thing online. A letter from the pope."

She put down a bean. She looked at the screen a long moment, then at him. "Paenitemini," she said. "That's the one. Nineteen sixty-six."

He waited, but she only started on the beans again, so he read. Pope Paul VI, in that year, had allowed the national conferences of bishops to replace the traditional Friday fast and abstinence with other forms of penance. Prayer. Works of charity. He read the sentence twice, and something in his chest went loose and then immediately tight again, because now he had the opposite problem. If the rule could be replaced, why did his grandmother still keep it? And if she kept it anyway, was the rule really gone, or just hiding?

"So it doesn't apply anymore," he said. "That's my whole case, right there."

"That's not what I said."

"You didn't say anything."

"I said your grandfather liked it." She tipped the beans into the colander and ran water over them. "The pope let the bishops change the penance. He didn't say Fridays stopped meaning anything."

He wanted her to expatiate on that, to go on until the whole shape of it was laid out for him, and she knew it, and she refused. She dried her hands on the dish towel and told him to watch the rice. That was the entire lesson she would give.

He watched the rice. He also texted Theodore, because the rules of the debate allowed cross-examination and Dominic intended to use it. Do you think the rule binds everyone or just people whose bishops kept it? Theodore's reply came back fast: binds everyone, it's the tradition, one church not fifty. Dominic typed and deleted three answers. He was beginning to see that "the rule doesn't apply" and "the rule applies but differently here" were not the same claim, and that he had been arguing the first while living, every Friday of his life, inside the second.

Ms. Kelly had told the class that the strongest position was often the one you could hold while looking at the counterargument straight on, and Dominic had nodded that day without really knowing what she meant. He thought he knew now. At lunch the next day he asked Paul outright whether his family did any Friday penance at all, and Paul shrugged and said his mom volunteered at the shelter on Fridays, had been doing it since Paul was little, called it her penance, which Paul thought was a joke until Dominic repeated the words back to him and watched him consider, for the first time, that it might not be.

The night before the debate, Dominic sat at the kitchen table with his notes while his grandmother oiled a loaf pan. He had structured it three ways and torn apart two of them. The position he had left was narrower than the one he'd wanted: that the old rule, as a universal command, no longer applied as it once had, because the Church itself had opened the door in 1966, and the national bishops had walked through it differently; but that this did not make Friday empty, because something had been substituted for the abstaining, and the substituting was itself the rule now. He could defend that. He could not defend the claim that nothing had changed, because his grandmother's Fridays and Paul's mother's Fridays had both changed the shape of the same thing, and he was not sure, honestly, whether that meant the rule was dead or alive.

"Is it tenable?" his grandmother asked, nodding at the notes. She had a way of finding the exact word and using it like a spoon, to stir something.

"I don't know yet. Ask me tomorrow."

She slid the pan into the oven and set the timer. "Bring me the pepper, then," she said. "And tell me what you're going to say when Theodore asks about the hamburger."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA advises reheating leftovers to an internal temperature of 74 degrees Celsius (165 degrees Fahrenheit).
story:
The thermometer had come from the back of her mother's kitchen drawer, a slender metal probe with a dial the size of a watch face, and Annabelle carried it through the farmers' market like something she might be asked to explain. She had planned the week on graph paper, six dinners, one night of leftovers engineered in, and now she was executing the plan, which was a word she had started using that made Delphine laugh at her. Delphine walked beside her with a canvas bag already heavy with plums, eating one as she went.

"You bought a kilogram of rice," Delphine said, looking into Annabelle's basket. "That's not a meal, that's a siege."

"It's the base for three of the dinners. You cook it all at once, in a batch, and then you reheat it across the week." Annabelle had read this in a book her aunt had lent her, a book with chapters on planning and shopping and cooking ahead, and the logic of it had appealed to her the way a well-built proof did: nothing wasted, everything sequenced. Her mother had been laid up since the surgery, tired in a way that debilitated her whole day rather than any single hour, and the household had been living on whatever could be assembled in ten minutes. Annabelle had decided, privately, that she would take over the cooking. Not dramatically. Just for the week, to see if she could.

At the egg stall Yannick was working the till for his uncle, and he rang up her dozen without a receipt, sliding the carton across. "You're the batch girl," he said. "Delphine told me. Rice and beans, rice and vegetables, rice and something else."

"Rice and eggs," Annabelle said. "Thursday."

"It's all rice to me." He shrugged, friendly, and called the next customer.

The problem arrived at the fish stall, where Mr. Silva, who lived three houses down and sold mussels pulled from the flats most mornings, was shoveling ice over his stock with a wooden scoop. He had a way of watching customers decide, patient, as though the mussels would still be there however long they took. Annabelle had mussels penciled in for Friday, and she asked him for a kilogram, and then, because the rice question had been circling her all morning, she asked him something else.

"When you reheat things," she said, "how do you know they're hot enough?"

Mr. Silva set down the scoop. "For mussels, you know by when they open. Rice, I'd use a thermometer." He nodded at her pocket, where the probe's dial showed at the edge like a coin in a purse. "My daughter checks everything with one of those. She's careful." He weighed the mussels without hurry, seawater dripping back into the tray. "There's a number for it, for reheating. She has it written on the fridge."

He didn't say the number. Annabelle bought the mussels and walked on, and it bothered her, the gap where the fact should be, like a word she had known the shape of all her life without ever learning it.

At home, in the narrow afternoon kitchen, she laid out her purchases and thought about the two things she was carrying. Her aunt's book treated cooking like logistics: a system, inputs and outputs, the whole week solved on one page. Her mother, before the surgery, had cooked by feel, a palm flat over a pan, a pinch of this, heat judged by the sound of it, and it had always worked. Annabelle had assumed for a while that the two ways were opposed, and now she wasn't sure. Her mother's way was quiet knowledge accumulated in the hands. The book's way was numbers written down so a stranger could follow. Maybe they were not opposites so much as the same care in different formats, though she couldn't yet say where one ended and the other began.

She cooked the rice in the big pot, cooled it in shallow trays as the book instructed, portioned it into containers, and labeled them with the days. Then, on Wednesday evening, reheating Wednesday's portion, she took out the thermometer and found she did not know what number she was waiting for. She pushed the probe into the middle of the rice and watched the dial climb, and the dial was indifferent to her, climbing slowly, and she had to decide what would count as done.

She looked it up on her phone while the steam rose. The USDA advised reheating leftovers to an internal temperature of 74 degrees Celsius, which the screen also gave as 165 degrees Fahrenheit. She read the sentence twice, then set the phone face down and watched the dial instead. It passed 60. It passed 70. At 74 she pulled the probe out, and the rice was steaming and smelled like nothing in particular, which was its own small disappointment, and she mixed in the beans and the caramelized onions she had made on Sunday.

Her mother ate slowly at the table, one hand keeping the bowl steady. "This is good," she said. "The onions especially."

"Onions were Delphine's idea. She said it wasn't a meal without them." Annabelle sat down across from her. "It's semantics, really, whether Sunday counts as part of Wednesday's dinner or its own thing. I cooked it all at once but we're eating it in pieces."

"Most weeks are like that," her mother said, and took another spoonful.

After the dishes, Annabelle opened the fridge and looked at the remaining containers, Thursday through Saturday, each labeled in her handwriting, each one a claim that the future could be portioned in advance. She still didn't know if the food would taste the same on Saturday as it had tonight, or whether her mother would be well enough by then to cook again, which would make all this unnecessary, which would be wonderful. She pinned the temperature to the fridge with a magnet, 74 Celsius, 165 Fahrenheit, the way Mr. Silva's daughter had done, and stood back to look at it.

Delphine texted a photograph of the littoral path by her grandmother's house, all grey sky and wet sand, with the caption, plums eaten, siege beginning. Annabelle laughed, typed back Thursday, rice and eggs, come hungry, and set out the pan for the morning.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The stage manager records the blocking in the prompt book so that it can be repeated the same way at every performance.
story:
The living room of his grandfather's house smelled of lavender and old radiator dust, and Luca had decided this made it a theatre. He pushed the armchairs against the wall, taped an X on the floorboards with painter's tape, and stood on the ottoman. "Places," he said, and felt something in his chest go bright and terrified at once.

The one-act was called The Littoral Hours, twenty minutes of two characters arguing on a beach at dawn, which Luca had chosen mostly because it required no set beyond a blue bedsheet and a paper sun. Sylas had been cast as the tide-obsessed younger brother. Calum played the older one, a lighthouse keeper who kept a ledger of everything the sea had taken from him. Their first rehearsal was a disaster of the ordinary kind: both of them walked wherever they pleased, gestured like men swatting flies, and blocked each other from the imaginary water.

"You malign my process," Calum said when Luca told him his crossing to the window looked like a man fleeing a bee.

"Your process is walking in circles," Luca said. "There are no circles. There is a beach. It is a beach with geography."

Sylas, who was lying on the bedsheet eating dry cereal from his pocket, raised a hand. "I have a question about the hermeneutics of the thing. When the script says he moves away, is that away from the brother or away from the sea? Because those are opposite directions."

It was, annoyingly, a good question, and Luca didn't have an answer, so he made a decision instead, which he was beginning to understand was most of directing. Away from the brother. He then spent ten minutes arranging their movement beat by beat, and by the end of it Calum's approach to the paper sun had a shape to it, an intention, and Luca stood on the ottoman feeling like a small god of a very small country.

The trouble came at the next rehearsal, when Calum came in and crossed left instead of right, and Sylas came in and crossed right instead of left, and they met in the middle of the beach like two delivery vans in a narrow street. "I was here last time," Calum said. "I remember the window."

"You were at the window the first time," Sylas said. "Then he moved you."

"I moved you both," Luca said, and realized, saying it, that he had moved them differently each time, improvising corrections he hadn't kept track of, and that his authority rested on a memory he did not actually have. He went quiet. In the hall his grandfather's shelf held boxes of old theatre programmes, and beneath them a fat black binder with a spine like a Bible, full of decades of somebody else's production. Luca turned the pages. Handwritten diagrams, arrows, initials in circles, the same scene drawn three times with tiny revisions, someone's pencil noting where everyone stood, night after night.

He carried it back in and put it in Sylas's hands. "You're the stage manager now. The blocking goes in the prompt book."

"What's a prompt book?"

"It's this. You write down every move we set, so it's the same every performance." Luca tapped the binder. "You are now the most powerful person in this living room. Do not let it go to your head."

It went, of course, directly to Sylas's head, and the days that followed had a new rhythm: they would set a cross, Sylas would sketch it in his notebook with the gravity of a court stenographer, and Calum would test him by inventing false memories of previous rehearsals, which Sylas would defeat by reading aloud from the page. On opening night, which was performed for an audience of two parents, one grandfather, and Mr. Popescu from next door, Calum dried in the middle of the second scene. He stood at the paper sun when he should have crossed to the bedsheet, and Sylas stood on the wrong side of the beach, arms out, stranded.

"I'm certain I come to you," Calum whispered, loud enough for the front row.

"You come to me," Sylas whispered back.

"Last night I came to you."

"Last night is not tonight. Look it up." Sylas nodded toward the wings, where the notebook lay open on the piano bench, and Calum, without breaking character entirely, managed to turn the pages as a man might consult a lighthouse ledger, which was, Luca thought, watching from the back with his arms crossed, the best piece of accidental staging they'd found all week. Calum read the little diagram, closed the book, and crossed to the bedsheet. The paper sun caught the lamp behind it and glowed along its littoral edge, and Luca leaned against the wall of his grandfather's house and whispered, "And scene."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Most US and Canadian jurisdictions use graduated licensing, in which new drivers move from a learner's permit to a provisional license with restrictions before a full license.
story:
The licensing office smelled like hand sanitizer and old carpet, and the number ticket in Anais's hand read B47, which meant she had time to memorize the poster about organ donation and then un-memorize it. She was here for her learner's permit, eighteen years old and the last of her friends to bother, mostly because her mother had offered, with what Anais considered munificent timing, to pay for lessons if Anais got the permit before September. A free road test and forty dollars a week saved: that was the kind of generosity that arrived exactly when it was convenient for everyone.

Two rows over, a boy in a basketball jersey was arguing with the clerk at Window 3. He had his permit in his fist, still warm from the printer, and the trouble seemed to be that he had expected the plastic card to work like a key. "So I can just drive my boys home from practice," he was saying, and the clerk, patient in the way of someone who had this conversation forty times a week, kept shaking her head.

Anais hadn't meant to eavesdrop, but the office was small and the boy was loud. "You have the learner's permit now," the clerk said. "That's stage one. Stage two is a provisional license, and it comes with restrictions before you get the full license. No friends in the car yet, not at this stage." The boy slumped against the counter like a tent losing its poles. Anais turned back to the organ donor poster and felt something rearrange itself quietly in her head. She had assumed a permit was a permit was permission. Apparently the system believed in stages, in earning trust one restriction at a time, which was either insulting or sensible depending on the minute.

She thought of her friend Nyla, who had been driving alone since spring and acted as though the skill had arrived in her fully formed, like a birthmark. Nyla had never mentioned stages. Hope, who took the bus everywhere on principle, would say the whole structure was designed to preempt freedom itself, that restrictions multiplied like mold in a student fridge. Anais had spent most of her life choosing between those two voices, the breezy and the suspicious, and had lately begun to suspect that neither of them had actually read anything.

Window 4 opened. "B47," said a man with reading glasses pushed up into his hair, and Anais went up, handed over her documents, and passed the written test on the second try after missing a question about backing out of driveways. Then a man named Mr. Tse, the instructor her mother had hired, collected her from the bench with the unhurried manner of someone who had taught approximately four thousand neophytes to operate a two-ton machine and had stopped being surprised by any of them. "You'll be nervous for eleven minutes," he said. "Then you'll be too busy to be nervous. It's a very efficient system."

The car was a white sedan with a second brake pedal on the passenger side, which Mr. Tse called his "vote." She pulled out of the lot too gently, then too sharply, then found something in the middle. At the first red light he asked her a question that seemed unrelated: "That boy at Window 3. You heard him?" She said she had. "What do you think, is the system mean or kind?" She waited through the light change, checked the mirror twice, and said that it was probably mean in the way that a fence around a pool was mean. He made a sound that could have been approval or a cough.

She drove for forty minutes, and somewhere around minute eleven his prophecy came true and her hands stopped narrating their own movements. She was beginning, on her own and without either Nyla's confidence or Hope's suspicion, to hold two thoughts at once: that the restrictions on a new driver were genuinely annoying, and that she was, today, genuinely bad at controlling this car, and that a person who was genuinely bad at something probably should not yet be trusted with passengers she liked. Both thoughts fit in her head at the same time, which felt like a new capability, like depth perception arriving late. What she couldn't decide was where the line was, which month, which skill threshold, and she suspected no one could tell her exactly, which was either the system's honesty or its laziness.

On the drive back, the boy from Window 3 was at the bus stop out front, permit in his fist again, staring at it as though it had lied to him personally. Mr. Tse rolled down his window. "Stage two, kid," he called. "It comes faster than you think and slower than you want." The boy flipped the permit over, hunting for the fine print, and Anais signaled, checked her mirror, and eased out of the lot past him.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: DNA copying is semiconservative: each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand.
story:
The countdown timer on the fume hood read forty minutes, which was also how long Maelie had to decide whether to sign up for the regional biotech competition, because Ms. Kaur had set the sheet on the bench by the door and the sign-up line was closing at four o'clock. She was supposed to be making her model anyway, the one that would qualify her if she entered, a physical demonstration of how a gene becomes a protein, and so far she had a shoebox, a ball of red yarn, and a theory that she was in over her head.

"You're staring at that yarn like it insulted you," Parsa said, sliding onto the stool beside her. Across the room Jameson was bent over his own model, cages of pipe-cleaner ribosomes he refused to let anyone touch.

"It's the copying part," Maelie said. "Everything after makes sense to me. The strand gets read, a messenger carries it out, the ribosome links amino acids in order. That part I could teach. But the copying, I keep drawing it wrong."

Jameson looked up anyway. "Wrong how? It's not hard. The double helix untwists, the two strands separate, and each old strand builds its partner." He said it the way he said most things, as though the universe were embarrassed not to have occurred to him first.

"Except then what do you actually have at the end?" Parsa asked, and Maelie appreciated her for this, because Parsa asked the questions Maelie was too proud to. "Two helixes. Fine. But are they both new, or is there something of the original left in them? Ms. Kaur said the competition judges ask about that. The model has to show it."

Jameson shrugged. "Obviously they're new. Copies of copies. That's what copying means."

Maelie turned the yarn over in her fingers. She thought of her grandmother's recipe cards, recopied so many times the ink had gone through three generations of paper, until the original didn't exist anywhere and only the words survived. That was one way to imagine it. But she thought too about the river behind her house, which was never the same water and never a different river, and she suspected DNA was more like the river than the recipe card, though she couldn't have said why the suspicion was worth anything. Her psychology teacher had a word for watching your own thinking like this, metacognition, and had claimed it improved performance on exams. Maelie found it mostly improved her awareness of how little she knew.

She took two colors of yarn to the front bench and began. One long blue strand, twisted with one long white, a ladder split down the middle and laid flat. On the whiteboard she drew what Jameson claimed: the blue and white separating, two new molecules assembling, both of them gleaming and unfamiliar, the original gone. It looked clean. It was also, she realized slowly, wasteful, an entire molecule discarded and rebuilt from nothing, and if her physics unit had taught her anything it was that cells were rarely so extravagant. The parsimonious answer, the one that threw nothing away, would be for each separated strand to keep serving as a pattern right where it stood. She picked up the blue strand and wound new white yarn against it. Then the original white, and new blue beside it. Two molecules, each of them half old and half new.

"That's not what I said," Jameson said, appearing at her elbow with his pipe cleaners.

"No," Maelie said. "It's not." Her hands were slow now, deliberate, because she could feel the idea balancing on something thin and she didn't want to knock it off by hurrying. She held up the two finished yarn helixes, one blue-and-new-white, one white-and-new-blue. "Every copied molecule keeps one strand from the original, and the new strand gets built to pair with it. Nothing's thrown away. The old strand isn't a copy left behind, it's half of every daughter molecule."

Parsa frowned. "Semiconservative," she said. "I saw the word in the textbook last night and skipped it because it looked like it would be boring."

"It means exactly this," Maelie said, and laughed, because the word had looked boring to her too. Jameson went back to his bench without a word, and for a while there was only the sound of tape being pulled and torn, and the tick of the fume hood timer, eleven minutes now. Ms. Kaur came by and turned Maelie's two helixes over in her hands, once, twice, and set them down without correcting anything, which among the students in that lab counted as applause.

At 3:52 Maelie walked to the door with her pen already uncapped. She still didn't know how she'd show the transcription step, the messenger peeling away and carrying its code out of the nucleus, and she had no idea whether she could stand at a judges' table in six weeks and hold her own against Jameson, who would certainly enter and certainly not make it easy. She looked at the sign-up sheet, and at her name half-written above the line, and at the blue yarn still caught around her wrist where she hadn't bothered to unwind it.

"Maelie," Parsa called from the bench, holding up the spare scissors. "You forgot these."

"I didn't forget," Maelie said, and finished signing her name.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A dot after a note adds half the note's value, so a dotted half note lasts three beats in 4/4 time.
story:
The basement of St. Brigid's smelled of candle wax and old carpet, and on Thursday evenings it belonged to the young composers' workshop that Ms. Vu ran after choir practice, unpaid, because she believed the church organ deserved better than the same eight hymns forever. Natalie had come for the first time in October, embarrassed to be there, clutching a notebook of half-finished melodies she'd never played for anyone. Now it was December, and Ms. Vu had assigned the most difficult thing yet: sixteen bars, with chord changes, written out properly in standard notation. No more humming into her phone and hoping.

She sat at the folding table nearest the radiator, which clanked like a percussion instrument nobody had asked for. Across from her, Christophe bent over his own staff paper, tapping his pencil in fours. He was the confident one, the one who had played piano since he was six and spoke about voicings the way other people spoke about weather. Natalie had spent most of the term deciding he was a charlatan, all vocabulary and no feeling, and then one evening in November he'd played a four-bar phrase so plain and so sad that she'd had to look away. Since then she'd been less sure of her judgments, which she found inconvenient.

The rules of the assignment circumscribed everything: sixteen bars exactly, in 4/4, at least three chord changes, and it had to be performable by the two of them on the church's upright piano at the Advent concert. Ms. Vu had said the deadline was non-negotiable because the concert program was already at the printer's. Natalie had agreed easily, the way she agreed to things, and then spent two weeks discovering that a melody she could hear perfectly in her head turned to water the moment she tried to write it down. The notes were fine. It was the time that kept betraying her, the arithmetic of beats, which seemed to belong to a different part of her brain than the part where the music lived.

Her phone buzzed against the table. A message from Alex, who had quit the workshop in November and texted like someone watching from a window.

heard you're playing at the concert. i quit because ms vu made me feel stupid, not gonna lie. but i still write stuff at home. how do you even make a melody come out right on paper? mine always sounds like a math problem.

Natalie typed back under the table, feeling the small disloyalty of it. mine sounds like a math problem too. that's kind of the whole thing. she put the phone face down before Ms. Vu could see, though Ms. Vu saw everything and mostly chose not to mention it.

Then Christophe said a quiet curse and turned his paper sideways, as if the problem were one of orientation. "Third bar," he said. "It keeps coming out wrong." He played it, and Natalie heard it immediately, a hole where the sound should have been. His bar had a half note and then a quarter note, and then nothing, a silence that dropped the melody on its back.

"You're a beat short," she said.

"I know I'm a beat short. I've been a beat short for twenty minutes." He glared at the staff paper. "I could chop the melody up, I suppose, make everything littler."

Natalie looked at his bar, at the half note sitting there with its empty space after it, and something shifted in her with a force that felt almost seismic, though nothing in the room moved. A half note was two beats. And after it, on the page, a dot. She remembered the page from the theory book Ms. Vu had lent her, remembered thinking it was a smudge at first. A dot after a note adds half the note's value, so a dotted half note lasts three beats. Two beats plus half of two. Three. She had read it and forgotten it, and now it arrived back whole.

"Put a dot after the half note," she said. "A dotted half note lasts three beats in 4/4. Your bar's only got three beats in it, right? Two and one. Add the dot and the half note takes all three."

Christophe looked at her, then at the paper, then drew the dot with a tiny deliberate press of the pencil. He played the bar again and it filled, the note stretching warm and long over the space that had been empty, and his melody finally had room to breathe. He played it twice more, as if checking that it hadn't been an accident.

"Where did you learn that?" he said.

"The book Ms. Vu gave me. I thought it was trivia when I read it." She pulled her own paper toward her and looked at bar eleven, the bar she'd been avoiding all evening, where her melody kept cramming itself into smaller notes because she hadn't known there was another way. She pencilled in a dotted half note, held the G for its three long beats, and let the phrase settle over the C chord underneath it like something landing.

Ms. Vu came over during the last fifteen minutes and played both their melodies through, once each, without comment. At the door, handing back the papers, she paused over Natalie's bar eleven. "Sing it to me on Sunday before I decide," she said, which was not a yes and not a no.

Outside, the cold hit her face, and she texted Alex while waiting for the bus: it's still a math problem. but tonight the math did what i wanted for once. She stood under the streetlamp with her notebook under her arm, humming bar eleven, stretching the third beat out as long as the traffic would let her.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In US college admissions, a college's yield is the percentage of students it admits who then accept the offer and enroll.
story:
Ava had checked her email eleven times during first period, which was possible only because Ms. Suryanto had turned her back to write discussion questions on the board. The admissions office at Belford had said mid-December. It was December fourteenth. Beside her, Talan slid a folded note across the lab table: did you hear yet.

She shook her head and underlined the date in her notebook so hard the pen tore the page. Belford was the school her mother called the one that matters, the school with the tower on the brochure that her grandfather had supposedly almost attended before he absconded from his village with nothing but a suitcase. The story changed every time it was told. In some versions there had been a scholarship. In the version Ava preferred, there had been nothing, only nerve.

"You're going to wear a hole in that page," Talan whispered.

"I'm annotating."

"You're spiraling."

Ms. Suryanto turned around. "Since we're all so energetic this morning, let's use it. Belford sends its decisions today, doesn't it, Ava." It wasn't a question, and half the class turned to look at her, which Ava felt like weather, a cold front moving through. Ibraheem, two rows over, gave her a small thumbs up. He had applied early too, somewhere in the Midwest, and had already heard. He refused to say what the letter said, only that it was paper.

The discussion questions were about gerrymandering, which was Ms. Suryanto's way of teaching everything at once. "Is a system fair," she asked, "when it works exactly as designed?" Talan argued that design was the whole problem, that whoever drew the lines got to choose the voters, and that any populist promising to fix it was usually just promising to draw them himself. Ibraheem said that was too jaundiced, that institutions could be corrected from inside. Ava took notes and heard none of them. She was thinking about a different system, the one that would open a file with her name on it and move it into one of two piles.

At lunch she checked her phone in the stairwell where the wifi worked. There it was, from Belford, subject line: An Update on Your Application. Not congratulations, not regret. An update. She stood with her thumb over it for a long moment, then opened it, because Talan was climbing the stairs toward her and she didn't want an audience either way.

Deferred. They had moved her to the regular pool. They wished her a strong senior year.

"They didn't say no," Talan said, reading over her shoulder.

"They didn't say anything." She sat down on the step. "It's like being told maybe for three more months."

Ibraheem arrived with his tray and, in the spirit of full disclosure, finally admitted his letter: accepted, with a scholarship that covered tuition if he enrolled. "But here's the thing," he said, and he leaned in like he was sharing contraband. "On the tour, the guide kept bragging about their yield. I didn't know what it meant, so I asked."

"And?"

"Yield is the percentage of students a college admits who accept the offer and enroll. That's all it is."

Ava turned the sentence over. Percentage of admits who say yes. So a college could love being wanted and hate being doubted, could read a deferral not as mercy but as a hedge, a way to see who came back. She had been thinking of the decision as a judgment on her, a grade. But there was another way to hold it: she was also choosing, also holding an offer open or closed, and the college was simply guessing, like anyone, about who would stay.

"Mine's still a maybe," she said slowly. "But a maybe means I still get a vote."

"For three months," Talan said.

"For three months." She looked at the deferred letter again, then at the four other colleges on her list, the ones without towers, the ones nobody in her family had myths about. She had applied to them like buying insurance, barely looking at the policies.

Ms. Suryanto found her after last period, erasing the board with the inefficient thoroughness of someone buying time. "You went quiet in class," she said.

"I got deferred."

"Ah." The eraser stopped. "Well. You have until spring to decide what you actually want, which is more than most people get."

Ava walked out to the bus loop with her phone in her pocket, not in her hand. She took out a pen and wrote on the back of her hand, where she couldn't ignore it: visit the other four. Then, underneath, smaller: want, not tower. The bus hissed up to the curb, its doors folding open, and she stepped on.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that everyone aged 13 to 64 be tested for HIV at least once as part of routine health care.
story:
Ella had signed up to run the Tuesday peer health session at the community center mostly because Ms. Nkosi had looked desperate, and because Dominick had said, "You're the only one of us who can say the word clinic without giggling." That was not erudition, exactly, but it was a qualification. Now she sat in the waiting room of the Riverside Family Practice with a folder on her lap, waiting for her own seventeen-year checkup, and trying to turn a duty into a plan. If she was going to stand in front of eleven teenagers on Tuesday and explain consent, contraception, and how to actually get tested for infections, she figured she should first learn what a clinic visit felt like from the inside.

The nurse called her back, weighed her, and took her blood pressure while asking about school. Then, at the end, almost as an afterthought, the nurse said, "We also offer an HIV test today. It's routine."

"Routine," Ella repeated, which made her sound like a slow student, but she was genuinely startled. "Like, for everyone? Not because of anything?"

"The CDC recommends everyone ages thirteen to sixty-four get tested for HIV at least once, as part of routine health care," the nurse said, already clicking through the screen. "So yes. Everyone."

Ella agreed to the test, partly because refusing felt like admitting something, and partly because she had a Tuesday session to think about. The swab was quick and tasteless and entirely undramatic, which was itself a revelation. In the exam room afterward, she asked the doctor, Ms. Nkosi, whether she could take some pamphlets. "For a peer education thing," she said, and then, feeling her ears go warm, "I have to explain consent on Tuesday, and I've never explained it out loud, only read it."

Ms. Nkosi gave her a stack of pamphlets and a look that Ella could not decode, somewhere between amusement and respect. In the waiting room afterward, waiting the twenty minutes for her result, Ella found Dominick and Angelo, who had nominally come to "support" her but had really come for the pharmacy milkshakes next door. She spread the pamphlets across three chairs like a general with a moribund campaign and a fresh map.

"Okay," she said. "Practice audience. Consent. Say someone wants to kiss someone. What has to happen?"

"A conversation," said Angelo, with surprising speed.

"Enthusiastic and ongoing," said Dominick, who had apparently read the pamphlet over her shoulder.

"Contraception," Ella continued, flipping pages. "There's more than condoms, which I did not know. There's a whole shelf of options, and a clinic will walk you through them without telling your parents, depending on the state, which I have to check." She paused. "And testing. Here's the part I got wrong this morning. I thought you only got tested if something was wrong. But they offered me an HIV test like it was a flu shot. The CDC says everyone thirteen to sixty-four, at least once, just as part of routine care. Not because of anything."

"Everyone?" said Angelo. "Like me?"

"Like you," said Ella. "Like the entire waiting room."

From the doorway behind them, Ms. Nkosi watched the whole small circus unfold. She had been a physician for nineteen years and had learned to read a waiting room the way sailors read weather: the slumped man with the cough, the mother scrolling her phone with one eye on her daughter. This trio she had not predicted. The girl was teaching, actually teaching, holding up a pamphlet on contraception and saying, "No, look, it's a spectrum, not a single method," while the two boys leaned in like she was describing a heist. Ms. Nkosi had prepared a gentle speech about the peer session, some words to assuage the girl's nerves before Tuesday, a small sermon about how knowledge shared was knowledge doubled. She now saw the speech was unnecessary, which was its own kind of good news, and slightly deflating, since she had rehearsed it in the car.

She crossed the waiting room with the printout in her hand. "Ella. Negative," she said, and watched the girl's shoulders drop an inch, relief arriving before pride could catch up.

"That's for me," Ella said, "but everyone thirteen to sixty-four should hear the part about it being routine. At least once. Routine health care." She turned to the boys. "That's the slide. That's literally the slide."

Dominick raised his milkshake. "To routine health care."

Ms. Nkosi folded her arms, feeling her rehearsed speech dissolve entirely. "Ms. Ella," she said, "before Tuesday, would you consider a return engagement? My Thursday parenting class has questions I keep answering badly. You seem to answer better."

"Badly how?" said Ella.

Ms. Nkosi sighed. "Last month a father told me abstinence pamphlets were moribund and I said, 'Define that,' and he did, correctly, and I had nothing."

Angelo choked on his milkshake. Ella looked at the pamphlets, then at the clock, then at Ms. Nkosi's face, which was, unmistakably, hopeful.

"Tuesday first," Ella said. "But bring the dad."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby.
story:
Angelina had chosen the coffee shop because it was halfway between her house and his, which felt fair, and because she knew the corner table by the window was free on weekday afternoons, which felt safe. She arrived twelve minutes early, ordered a chai, and then watched a cyclist clip the curb outside and come down hard on the pavement right in front of her. She was out the door before the drink was finished, kneeling on the sidewalk with her napkins while the man sat up, dazed, a scrape opening red along his elbow.

He was fine, mostly. A woman from the pharmacy brought antiseptic wipes, and Angelina held the man's phone while he called his wife, and by the time the ambulance he didn't really need had been waved away, her heart was slamming against her ribs so hard she could feel it in her throat. Back inside, the barista had kept her chai warm and had set a plate of shortbread beside it. "On the house," the barista said. "That was kind, what you did." Angelina thanked her, sat down at the corner table, and realized her hands would not stop trembling.

Which was a problem, because Kaeden walked in ninety seconds later.

They had met in Ms. Côté's psychology seminar, where he sat two rows behind her and argued, cheerfully and at length, about whether empathy could be taught. He was wearing the grey jacket she recognized from class, and he was carrying a paperback he'd promised to lend her, and the sight of him made her pulse do something she was almost sure was not about him at all. She had read about this. Her older sister had taken a night course and had come home evangelizing about it, determined to proselytize the whole family, and one phrase had stuck.

"Hi," Kaeden said, setting the book down. "You're early."

"I helped a guy who fell off his bike," she said. "Outside. He's okay. But I'm kind of wired." Then, because she'd decided on the walk over that she wasn't going to be someone who performed calm, she added, "My sister took this psych course. She says psychologists call it misattribution of arousal, when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement gets mistaken for attraction to the person nearby."

Kaeden laughed, caught off guard, and then considered it seriously, which was the thing she liked about him. "So your heart is racing right now," he said, sitting down, "and you can't tell if it's me or the cyclist."

"Exactly. It's an unfalsifiable situation." She wrapped her hands around the chai to steady them. "I'm an aesthete about first dates, I think. I like the ritual of them. But this one's contaminated."

He flagged the barista and ordered coffee, and when it came he pushed his sugar across to her without being asked, because she'd once mentioned in class that she took sugar in everything and he had apparently filed it away. That smallness undid her more than she expected. "Okay," she said. "Honest experiment. If it's the accident, my pulse should settle in a few minutes and then we can see what's left."

They talked while she waited to feel the adrenaline drain: about Ms. Côté's impossible essay question on memory, about the man on the curb, about how he volunteered at the shelter downtown and had started seeing the same indigent men week after week until they weren't a category anymore, just Dale who liked westerns and Marcus who'd been a machinist. She told him about her sister's diagnosis two years ago and the winter she'd spent being the person who drove to appointments. He listened the way he argued, completely.

By the time her cup was half empty, her hands had gone still, and she took inventory, as though checking pockets. Her heart was beating normally. What remained was something quieter and more specific: the fact that she wanted to keep sitting here, that she was already half composing the text she'd send Elaina tonight, that she'd noticed he'd turned his chair a few degrees toward the window when the light shifted so the sun wouldn't be in her eyes.

"So?" Kaeden said. "What's the verdict?"

"The verdict is I can't fully separate them, and I'm not going to pretend I can," Angelina said. "But I'd like to do this again somewhere without ambulances. Maybe the bookshop."

He slid the paperback across the table, and she saw he'd dog-eared a page for her, a passage he'd already picked out. "It's a date," he said.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: The term 'unreliable narrator' was coined by the critic Wayne C. Booth in his 1961 book The Rhetoric of Fiction.
story:
Mr. Takahashi handed the essays back in reverse alphabetical order, which meant Cohen waited through the whole stack, watching classmates fold their papers or skim their margins while pretending not to. When his reached him, a red circle sat around one phrase near the top of the second page: "unreliable narrator." Beside it, in cramped handwriting, was a single question. Where does this term come from?

He had written it without thinking, the way he wrote most of what he knew. The novel was about a drowned girl and the cousin who insisted, chapter after chapter, that he had warned her about the ice. Cohen's essay argued that the cousin's version of events couldn't be trusted because every detail he remembered placed himself in the right. He'd felt clever writing it. Now the question made the phrase feel borrowed, like a jacket he'd found somewhere and worn so long he'd forgotten it wasn't his.

At lunch he found Beatrice at the corner table, her own essay spread out, annotated in three colors. "Did he circle yours?" he asked.

"He circled my thesis and wrote 'braver than true,'" she said. "Why, what did you get?"

"Where does this term come from. As if I invented it or something."

"Maybe he wants to know if you know." She slid a library copy of the novel across the table so he could see her marginal notes. She had underlined every sentence where the cousin described his own kindness. "Look at this part. He says he offered her his coat. Then later he says he would have offered her his coat if he'd thought of it. Both can't be true, and he doesn't even notice he's said both."

Hunter dropped into the seat across from them, still holding his economics workbook. "Don't ask me about stagflation," he said, before either of them could speak. "Prices going up while the economy stalls, and Mr. Rowley expects us to explain it in a paragraph. It's like being asked to explain why water is wet."

"It's not like that at all," Beatrice said.

"It's exactly like that."

Cohen wasn't listening. He had turned back to his essay, and the question was still sitting there. After school he went to the library and asked the librarian for books about fiction, about criticism, and she walked him to a shelf he had never noticed, near the poetry no one borrowed. He pulled volumes down and put them back. Most of them assumed he already knew what he was looking for.

He found it on his fourth try, a dense book with a plain cover. He wasn't searching for his exact phrase; he was flipping through the index of a different volume when the name appeared as a cross-reference, pointing him here, to a chapter about the distance between the author and the voice telling the story. In the text, the critic Wayne C. Booth had given that distance a name, in a book called The Rhetoric of Fiction, published in 1961. Cohen read the sentence twice, then copied the page number onto his palm with the stub of a pencil, because his phone was dead and he did not trust himself.

The next morning he arrived early to Mr. Takahashi's classroom. The teacher was erasing the board, and the smell of chalk dust filled the room the way it does when no one else is there yet.

"I found it," Cohen said. "The term 'unreliable narrator.' It was coined by the critic Wayne C. Booth, in his 1961 book The Rhetoric of Fiction."

Mr. Takahashi set the eraser down. "And did you read any of it, or just the sentence?"

"Some of it. He talks about how the author and the narrator aren't the same person, so the author can let the narrator be wrong on purpose." Cohen realized he was starting to gesticulate, both hands out like he was holding the idea open for inspection, and he made himself put them on the desk. "But here's what I can't figure out. If the author wants us to doubt the cousin, why not just say so? Why make us do the work?"

"Perhaps because the work is the point," Mr. Takahashi said. "Or perhaps because a reader who is fooled and then unfooled trusts their own judgment more than a reader who is told. What do you think?"

"I think it's both. I think he hides it from readers who want to be hidden from." Cohen paused. "But I'm not sure how I'd prove that, and I'm not sure Booth would even agree with me."

The bell hadn't rung yet. Other students were drifting in, and Beatrice appeared in the doorway holding her annotated copy of the novel, scanning the room. Cohen sat down and opened his essay to the circled phrase, and in the margin, slowly, he began to write the page number from his palm.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The coefficients in a balanced chemical equation give the ratio of moles that react, not the ratio of masses.
story:
Chase set the chemistry worksheet on the kitchen table between the fruit bowl and his mother's unopened mail, because those two objects marked the only clear space left. She was on the couch with her bad leg propped on a cushion, and he could hear the small struggle of her reaching for the remote without sitting up, so he got it for her before he sat down, and she said thanks without looking away from the ceiling.

The problem wanted this: given 50.0 grams of nitrogen and hydrogen reacting to form ammonia, how many grams of ammonia could you get. The equation was printed at the top, N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, balanced and waiting. Chase had done the conversion to moles in his head on the bus, or thought he had, and now he wrote his answer fast, wanting to be done before dinner so he could text Aubree about the weekend. Twenty minutes later his answer, 60.7 grams, came back circled in red with a single word in the margin that Ms. Goh must have written during her free period: masses?

Fynn was already at the kitchen door, knocking on the frame of it because the door stood open. He came in without being asked twice, which was how he had operated since seventh grade, and he slid a chair around backwards and sat with his arms folded across its back. "She circled mine too," he said. "But mine's worse. I used grams the whole way through."

Chase pulled the worksheet closer and shielded his work with his forearm, an old reflex, then unshielded it, because Fynn had driven over on his bike in the dark partly for this. "What do you mean, grams the whole way through."

"In the ratio. One to three to two." Fynn tapped the coefficients. "I did 50 grams times two over one. Got a hundred grams of ammonia from fifty grams of stuff, which even I know is weird, because where would the extra fifty grams come from." His ears went red. "My uncle would say I invented matter."

Chase laughed, then stopped laughing, because his own answer was only wrong by a different amount and he could not yet say why. He had converted 50 grams to moles at the start. But then, at the ratio step, he had multiplied by two over one as if the two and the one were about grams. He stared at the line until it stopped looking like arithmetic and started looking like a decision he had made without noticing. His mother turned the television down a notch, which she did when she could tell he was working something out, and which she would never admit to doing.

"The coefficients," Chase said slowly, "are a ratio of moles. Not a ratio of masses." He said it to the page first, then said it again to Fynn, and watched Fynn's face do the same thing his own had probably done, a loosening followed almost at once by suspicion, because a truth that arrives too neatly can feel like a trick. "So you convert to moles first, then use the two to one, then convert back. The grams are just grams. They don't know about the equation."

"That's casuistry," Fynn said, meaning it as a joke, and Chase said no, casuistry was when you reasoned your way into something false with fine-sounding steps, and this was the opposite, this was the fine-sounding step being removed. Fynn argued for a minute that a ratio was a ratio, and Chase drew two rectangles on the margin of scrap paper, one labeled oxygen and one labeled gold, and asked whether one gram of each was the same amount of stuff, and Fynn said obviously not, gold was heavier, and then went quiet in the particular way he did when a thing landed.

They redid the problem together, Chase narrating and Fynn checking the arithmetic aloud, his finger moving along the line. Moles of nitrogen, then the two to one from the equation, then moles of ammonia, then molar mass, then grams. The answer came out different from before, smaller, and Chase checked it twice, not because he doubted Fynn's addition but because he had learned this week how easily a right method could still hide a wrong step. His mother called from the couch that there was soup if they wanted it, and Fynn said yes before Chase could make a judicious assessment of what was actually in the pot, and it turned out to be lentil, which was fine.

Over the bowls, Chase texted Aubree a photo of the corrected page, and she replied almost immediately: "wait that's what I did wrong on the quiz." Then a second message: "can I come over tomorrow." He typed yes and put the phone face down, and preempted the question he could see forming on Fynn's face by sliding the worksheet across the table. "Explain it to me," he said. "Without looking."

Fynn picked up the pencil, put it down, picked it up again. "The coefficients give you the ratio of moles that react. Not the ratio of masses. The masses are just, like, hanging around being heavy." He glanced up. "Is that it?"

"That's it," Chase said, and reached for the second bowl of soup.
